candidate_datasets.name: iNaturalist
candidate_datasets.role: Public plant photographs provide broad but mostly 2D observations of cymose inflorescences.

obstacles: Photographs often have perspective distortion and hidden shoots.
Successive lengths may vary with flowering stage and environment.
assessments.rationale: The mathematical conditions and curve fit are explicit. Public imagery can test visible scorpioid examples, while reliable 3D data for hidden helicoid geometry and representative taxonomic coverage are limited.

assessments.operationalization: Segment successive growth stages preserved by whorls or growth lines, rescale them and quantify shape similarity, terminal accretion and logarithmic-spiral fit. Systematic ontogenetic parameter change or a nonlogarithmic self-similar curve would refute the stated biological or uniqueness component.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: Open shell and horn scans preserve ontogenetic increments for similarity analysis.

obstacles: Shell ornament and damage affect registration.
The mathematical uniqueness statement depends on the precise definition of spiral and similarity.
assessments.rationale: Self-similarity and accretion geometry are direct measurements from abundant scans. Both biological constancy and the logarithmic model can be compared quantitatively against alternatives with standard methods.

assessments.operationalization: Partition accretionary structures at successive growth boundaries and test whether adding each increment produces a whole geometrically similar to the prior whole under one scale transformation. Deviations can be quantified by registered shape residuals.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: Open 3D scans of shells, horns and tusks allow gnomon and similarity tests.

obstacles: Growth boundaries may be incomplete or obscured.
Foraminiferal chambers can change shape during ontogeny.
assessments.rationale: The gnomon property has a direct geometric criterion and accretionary records are widely preserved. Existing 3D data can confirm or refute it across several named structure classes, though the word 'all' remains demanding.

assessments.operationalization: Sample curves from simultaneously formed soft outlines and incrementally accreted hard parts, fit logarithmic and rival models, and test association between accretion mode, logarithmic fit and visible growth lines. Credible logarithmic soft-tissue counterexamples would refute the exclusion.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: Open 3D media for accretionary hard-part curves.

candidate_datasets.name: iNaturalist
candidate_datasets.role: Large public image source for leaf margins, fish contours, claws and horns.

obstacles: Determining whether a part is formed simultaneously may require developmental knowledge.
Curve fitting is sensitive to landmark and scale selection.
assessments.rationale: The prediction contrasts observable structure classes and can be falsified by public morphology. Coverage is broad enough for a strong comparative test, although developmental mode must sometimes be assigned from external knowledge.

assessments.operationalization: Measure successive whorl breadths along homologous radii and test whether their ratios are constant, including whether Nautilus is near three. Compare geometric-progression residuals across nautiloids, ammonoids and gastropods.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: Open 3D and sectional shell models allow direct whorl-breadth measurement.

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: Public fossil metadata can support broad taxonomic sampling of ammonoids and nautiloids.

obstacles: Fossil deformation can alter whorl dimensions.
Species and ontogenetic stage sampling may be uneven.
assessments.rationale: This is an unusually direct quantitative claim with abundant preserved specimens and a clear refuting result. Standard morphometrics can evaluate both Nautilus's stated ratio and the broader generalization.

assessments.operationalization: Fit a generative shell model parameterizing aperture shape, expansion, rotation, translation and inclination to diverse univalve scans, then quantify unexplained shape variance and systematic residuals. The claim is supported if this parameter set reconstructs observed forms without additional qualitative mechanisms.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: Large open collection of 3D molluscan shell morphology for generative-model fitting.

obstacles: Ornament, aperture remodeling and local growth changes exceed the simple parameter set.
A flexible model can fit shapes without identifying biological causation.
assessments.rationale: Modern shell models make the proposed factors measurable and public scans offer broad coverage. The universal 'all differences' assertion and causal sufficiency are harder to discriminate because model flexibility and omitted ornament matter.

assessments.operationalization: Fit logarithmic spirals to shell whorls and estimate constant angles with uncertainty for Nautilus, ammonitoids and gastropods. Test Nautilus against about 80 degrees and estimate the fraction of ordinary taxa inside 80–85 degrees or below 80 degrees.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: Open shell scans enable direct estimation of spiral angles.

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: Fossil occurrence and taxonomy support representative ammonoid sampling.

obstacles: The terms 'ordinary' and 'typical' require a sampling definition.
Diagenetic deformation biases fossil measurements.
assessments.rationale: The numerical range is directly measurable from abundant living and fossil shells. Standard curve fitting and representative sampling can strongly confirm or refute the stated distribution.

assessments.operationalization: Estimate outer- and inner-border growth increments from shell growth geometry and regress whorl separation, contact and overlap against their ratio. Test whether other parameters such as aperture shape and translation improve prediction beyond that ratio.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: Open 3D shell scans provide whorl overlap and border-growth geometry.

obstacles: Static geometry only indirectly estimates growth rates.
Several shell-model parameters can affect apparent overlap.
assessments.rationale: The predicted association is quantitatively testable from existing scans. The word 'only' demands exclusion of correlated geometric factors, and inferred rates make that causal sufficiency less clean.

assessments.operationalization: Using independently inferred cephalopod phylogenies and stratigraphy, test whether spiral angle alone predicts ancestor-descendant order or primitiveness after accounting for size and clade. Frequent convergence and poor temporal prediction would support the warning against inference from angle alone.

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: Public fossil occurrences and ages for testing temporal order of shell forms.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: Open shell morphology for spiral-angle measurements.

obstacles: Independent fossil phylogenies remain uncertain.
The phrase 'no valid evidence' is methodological rather than a simple empirical frequency claim.
assessments.rationale: Existing fossil and morphology data can quantify how informative spiral angle is about age and descent. They cannot prove that angle provides no evidence in every model, but can resolve the historical series and convergence components.

assessments.operationalization: Estimate shell growth parameters along independently inferred lineages and test for sustained directional trends, while measuring homoplasy of similar parameter combinations across distant clades. Compare detection against qualitative morphology alone.

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: Public fossil chronology and taxonomy for directional-trend analyses.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: Open 3D shell data for quantitative growth parameters.

obstacles: Orthogenesis has multiple historical and modern meanings.
Directional trends may reflect sampling, selection or phylogenetic structure.
Independent phylogenies are incomplete for many fossil series.
assessments.rationale: Directional parameter change and convergence are measurable with public fossil morphology. The broad claim about what mathematical morphology can reveal is partly methodological, and attributing trends to orthogenesis requires substantial interpretation.

assessments.operationalization: Measure local spiral angle and whorl breadth through ontogeny in the named ammonoids and test whether increasing angle predicts narrowing while decline toward zero predicts uncoiling. Alternative local curve models provide direct comparison.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: Open fossil shell scans preserve ontogenetic coiling trajectories.

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: Public taxonomy and occurrences help identify and sample the named ammonoid groups.

obstacles: Fossil crushing can distort local angles.
Some named historical taxa have revised classifications.
assessments.rationale: The claim makes explicit within-shell quantitative predictions and fossils preserve the relevant trajectory. Existing scans and standard curve analysis can resolve the pattern in the named forms.

assessments.operationalization: Estimate spiral and apical angles from 3D specimens of Cerithium, Solarium, Natica and Planorbis, then partition intergeneric shape variance attributable to each. The claim predicts low variation in spiral angle and dominant variation in apical angle.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: Open 3D gastropod shell models enable direct angle and variance measurements.

obstacles: Within-genus species variation requires balanced sampling.
Aperture shape and ornament add differences not represented by the two angles.
assessments.rationale: Both quantities are directly measurable and the named common shell groups are represented in public collections. Variance decomposition gives a clear test of the comparative statement.

assessments.operationalization: Digitize successive growth lines on bivalve and brachiopod shells, test whether they share an umbonal axis, and fit circular, elliptical and direction-dependent growth models. Directional increment rates should quantitatively generate the observed line family.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: Open 3D shell surfaces allow extraction and fitting of growth lines.

obstacles: Fine growth lines may be below scan resolution.
Environmental interruptions can perturb otherwise regular line families.
assessments.rationale: The claim connects visible curves to explicit geometric growth models. Existing shell media can resolve the major pattern and named form differences using routine morphometrics.

assessments.operationalization: Use developmental imaging and preserved carapaces to test whether successive retained exuviae adhere as nested layers, project beyond prior margins and generate fitted logarithmic growth lines. Comparison with fully moulting branchiopods would test the incomplete-moult mechanism.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: Public micro-CT data may reveal nested carapace layers and external growth lines.

candidate_datasets.name: BioImage Archive
candidate_datasets.role: Potential open developmental microscopy of branchiopod moulting.

obstacles: Estheria is a historical taxonomic name.
Static carapaces may not distinguish retained moults from continuous secretion.
assessments.rationale: Nested layers and spiral lines are measurable, and the mechanism has a useful comparative prediction. Public developmental coverage of the relevant clam-shrimp taxa is likely too sparse for full causal resolution.

assessments.operationalization: Reconstruct shell interior and brachidium geometry across spire-bearing brachiopods, quantify shell elongation and flattening, and test the predicted association with outward, inward or discoid spiral direction. Phylogenetically controlled models should compare spatial constraint with clade-specific development.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: Open micro-CT models can preserve internal brachidia and external shell shape.

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: Public fossil taxonomy and occurrences support sampling across brachiopod groups.

obstacles: Internal brachidia are incompletely preserved.
Shell shape and arm direction are strongly confounded with phylogeny.
assessments.rationale: The association is directly testable with fossil 3D morphology, including the named form classes. Demonstrating that pressure and available space cause the pattern is less discriminating than documenting the predicted correlation.

assessments.operationalization: Combine fossil positional evidence, microstructure and independent cephalopod phylogenies to test homology between ammonite aptychi and dorsal shell components, and compare developmental boundary predictions from a split-cone model. Support requires congruent tissue homology and ancestral-state reconstruction.

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: Public ammonoid fossil occurrences and taxonomy for historical reconstruction.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: Open cephalopod fossil and shell scans for structural comparison.

obstacles: Soft-tissue attachment and embryonic stages are rarely preserved.
Deep homology alternatives can fit fragmentary fossil evidence.
The once-united ancestral structure is not directly observable.
assessments.rationale: Modern fossil and comparative data can test several consequences and likely reject or support homology hypotheses. The exact ancestral split event is a historical inference with incomplete preservation, preventing full resolution.

assessments.operationalization: Extract septal surfaces and attachment boundaries from 3D shells, solve the corresponding minimal-surface problem, and compare observed curvature and area with minimal, constant-mean-curvature and biomechanical alternatives. Shape classes should track boundary orientation as predicted.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: Open micro-CT shell volumes reveal internal cephalopod septa and attachment lines.

obstacles: Uniform pressure and isotropic membrane assumptions are not directly recorded.
Fossil deformation and later calcification can alter original septal shape.
assessments.rationale: Modern CT and numerical geometry permit a direct comparison of observed septa with boundary-matched surfaces. Mechanistic assumptions are not perfectly recoverable, but the core minimal-surface prediction is resolvable from existing data.

assessments.operationalization: Quantify branch topology, tip curvature and wavelength in ammonitic sutures and compare them with explicit surface-tension instability models and rival growth or buckling models. A surface-tension account must uniquely reproduce scaling and branching statistics, not merely visual resemblance.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: Open ammonite scans provide complex suture geometry.

obstacles: Pattern resemblance is non-unique across physical mechanisms.
Interfacial tensions during septum formation are not preserved.
Many fossils expose only 2D suture traces.
assessments.rationale: Suture morphology is abundant and measurable, but the analogical mechanism is weakly discriminating because reaction-diffusion, differential growth and buckling can produce similar branching. Existing data can test model fit, not confidently identify surface tension as the cause.

assessments.operationalization: Parameterize spiral shell form across molluscs, foraminifera and tube worms, then model recurrence and convergence against phylogeny, geological age, climate, depth and geography. The claim predicts frequent cross-group near-identity and weak environmental or temporal structure.

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: Public fossil occurrences through geological time and environments.

candidate_datasets.name: Ocean Biodiversity Information System
candidate_datasets.role: Public marine occurrence and environmental records for living shell-producing groups.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: Open 3D shell forms for quantitative similarity analysis.

obstacles: Morphology and occurrence databases require substantial taxonomic linkage.
Preservation and collecting biases vary strongly through time and habitat.
Claims about 'every' period and sea exceed actual coverage.
assessments.rationale: Large open fossil, occurrence and morphology resources address all major variables. They can test recurrence and environmental association broadly, but harmonization and severe sampling biases prevent literal resolution of the universal scope.

assessments.operationalization: Compare generative growth-only models and selection-aware evolutionary models against shell-form distributions, fitness proxies and phylogenetic transitions. Growth laws explain possibility, while evidence that form affects survival or reproduction would refute the strongest claim of no selective share.

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: Public fossil occurrence data can test differential persistence and transitions among shell forms.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: Open quantitative shell morphology for evolutionary model comparison.

obstacles: 'No necessary share' is a modal claim and cannot be proved by observational fit.
Growth constraints and natural selection are compatible rather than exclusive.
Fossil occurrence is an imperfect fitness proxy.
assessments.rationale: Existing data can test whether selection is associated with shell form and whether growth laws generate observed possibilities. They cannot resolve the non-necessity formulation cleanly, because a physical growth mechanism does not exclude evolutionary selection on its parameters.

assessments.operationalization: Segment unilocular shells in 3D, estimate their curvature and departures from constant-mean-curvature equilibrium shapes, and compare fits with constrained surface-tension models. Systematic agreement would support the proposed physical explanation; large structured departures would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: Public 3D specimen media that can supply shell geometry for some unilocular foraminiferal taxa.

obstacles: Static shell shape does not directly measure protoplasmic tension or conditions at solidification.
Open 3D coverage of unilocular taxa is sparse.
assessments.rationale: Shell geometry is measurable and equilibrium models are available, but translating Thompson's fluid-drop language into boundary conditions requires interpretation. Existing images can test shape compatibility, not cleanly identify surface tension as the cause.

assessments.operationalization: Reconstruct chamber-addition sequences from shell images and test whether exterior accretion with rigid retention predicts spiral trajectories better than alternative growth geometries. A consistent association between permanent external increments and spirality would support the claim, while abundant nonspiral shells under the same growth mode would weaken it.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: 3D shell scans for reconstructing chamber order and geometry.

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: Public fossil occurrence and taxonomic records for extending comparisons through time.

obstacles: The proposed condition may be permissive rather than sufficient.
Taxonomic and developmental coverage of digitized shell interiors is uneven.
assessments.rationale: Accretion sequence and spiral geometry can be measured in existing specimens. Observational morphology alone has limited power to separate this mechanism from developmental alternatives.

assessments.operationalization: Measure septal curvature and attachment boundaries in tomographic shells of Foraminifera and Nautilus, then compare observed surfaces with numerically computed minimum-area surfaces under inferred pressure orientation. Reversed curvature with good minimum-surface fits would support the claim; inconsistent orientation or poor fits would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: Open CT-derived shell geometry for cephalopods and some foraminifera.

obstacles: Pressure at septum formation is generally absent from museum datasets.
Preservation and scan resolution can distort thin septa.
assessments.rationale: The geometric predictions are explicit, and public tomography can test them for selected taxa. The causal pressure-side inference remains indirect and confounded by secretion and tissue support.

assessments.operationalization: Fit logarithmic and rival spiral models to chamber centroids and shell outlines across ontogenetic whorls, and test scale-invariant similarity of successive stages. Stable logarithmic parameters and superior fit support the claim; systematic parameter drift or better rival fits refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: Open 3D scans from which chamber trajectories and ontogenetic shell outlines can be measured.

obstacles: Internal chambers require tomography rather than exterior photographs.
Available scans may overrepresent conspicuous taxa.
assessments.rationale: This is a direct model-selection problem with clear geometric variables and standard methods. Public images and scans should resolve the assertion for a substantial, though not exhaustive, sample of spiral Foraminifera.

assessments.operationalization: Measure successive whorl breadths in digitized Fusulina sections, estimate ratios and spiral angles with uncertainty, and test constancy around 1.5 and 86 degrees. Confidence intervals excluding these values or showing ontogenetic drift would refute the numerical claim.

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: Public fossil records that identify collections and occurrences of fusulinids for targeted image compilation.

obstacles: PBDB occurrence records do not themselves contain whorl measurements.
Section orientation and fossil deformation can bias breadth ratios.
assessments.rationale: The exact ratio and angle give an unusually sharp test using standard morphometrics. Data are scattered among digitized fossil collections, so full species coverage may require compilation.

assessments.operationalization: Estimate volumes of successive chambers and test for a constant multiplicative ratio, then compare that pattern with any available longitudinal biomass or growth-rate series. Constant chamber ratios support the geometric component, but only proportional instantaneous biomass growth would support the stated cause.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: Tomographic shell media from which successive chamber volumes may be segmented.

candidate_datasets.name: PANGAEA
candidate_datasets.role: Public marine datasets that may provide cultured-foraminifera growth and environmental measurements.

obstacles: Fossil or museum shells lack instantaneous living mass and growth rate.
Constant ratios can arise from multiple developmental rules.
assessments.rationale: Existing scans can directly test chamber-size ratios. They cannot generally resolve whether proportional growth of homogeneous living mass caused those ratios.

assessments.operationalization: Fit minimum-energy chamber-shape models and proportional-size spiral models jointly to segmented shell ontogenies, comparing them with models based on fixed contact angle and biologically specified secretion. Better predictive fit across taxa would support the compound mechanism; failure of either component would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: 3D shell geometry for fitting chamber shape and spiral-growth models.

obstacles: Potential energy and boundary conditions are not observed directly.
Several mechanisms predict similar static chamber forms.
Open ontogenetic 3D series are limited.
assessments.rationale: The claim can be translated into physical models, but its broad minimum-potential wording permits many parameterizations. Static morphology offers only partial discrimination among the proposed and rival mechanisms.

assessments.operationalization: Classify species by attached benthic versus free planktonic habit and quantify planarity, attached-side flattening and helical displacement from shell scans. Strong habitat-associated differences after phylogenetic and size controls support the claim; no association or opposite patterns refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: World Foraminifera Database
candidate_datasets.role: Public taxonomy, distributions and ecological information for Foraminifera.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: 3D shell geometry for measuring flattening, planarity and helicity.

candidate_datasets.name: PANGAEA
candidate_datasets.role: Marine occurrence and assemblage datasets for ecological classification.

obstacles: Ecology is correlated with phylogeny and shell construction.
Many species lack public 3D scans.
assessments.rationale: Both habitat and shell geometry have clear modern operational definitions and public sources. Comparative data can test the association, although attributing it specifically to attachment force remains less decisive.

assessments.operationalization: Compare named morphospecies and genera using genomic delimitations, environmental time series and within-lineage shell morphometrics, especially in Peneroplis. Morphological forms repeatedly intergrading within one reproducing lineage would support the claim; stable genetically distinct lineages would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: NCBI Sequence Read Archive
candidate_datasets.role: Public sequence data for testing whether morphologically named forms belong to distinct genetic lineages.

candidate_datasets.name: World Foraminifera Database
candidate_datasets.role: Accepted names, synonymies and taxonomic scope for compiling comparisons.

candidate_datasets.name: PANGAEA
candidate_datasets.role: Environmental and assemblage series for testing environmentally induced form changes.

obstacles: Type material and sequence records are rarely linked to the same individuals.
The phrase 'temporary manifestations' can mean plasticity or life-cycle stages.
assessments.rationale: Integrative taxonomy can decisively test selected alleged species complexes with existing molecular and morphological records. Coverage is too uneven to settle Thompson's broad claim about many genera.

assessments.operationalization: Define fitness as lineage persistence or extinction risk and test whether shell-form traits predict survival across environmental transitions in fossil occurrence data. Detectable trait-dependent survival would refute the equal-fitness assertion, while no association under well-powered models would only weakly support it.

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: Public occurrence records for estimating foraminiferal lineage durations and extinction patterns.

candidate_datasets.name: PANGAEA
candidate_datasets.role: Marine sediment records connecting assemblage changes with environmental conditions.

obstacles: 'Simple laws' and fitness are not uniquely defined.
Fossil persistence is a noisy proxy for organismal fitness.
Preservation and sampling strongly confound form-dependent survival.
assessments.rationale: A restricted trait-dependent survival test is possible, but it captures only one meaning of fitness. The universal equality and proposed explanation are too broad to resolve cleanly with observational datasets.

assessments.operationalization: Map quantified shell forms onto independently inferred molecular and fossil phylogenies and count repeated origins of near-identical morphologies. Multiple distant lineages converging beyond uncertainty would support the claim; forms restricted to single clades would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: NCBI GenBank
candidate_datasets.role: Public sequences for phylogenies independent of shell shape.

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: Fossil occurrences for temporal tests of repeated morphotype origins.

candidate_datasets.name: World Foraminifera Database
candidate_datasets.role: Taxonomic backbone for linking names across sources.

obstacles: Sparse molecular sampling and uncertain fossil placement.
Identical form requires an explicit morphometric tolerance.
assessments.rationale: Convergence is testable when morphology is mapped onto a phylogeny inferred from independent characters. Existing data can establish examples but likely cannot estimate how often it happened across all Foraminifera.

assessments.operationalization: Relate measured shell strength and damage frequency to survival, reproduction and lineage persistence across environments, controlling for size and habitat. A positive fitness effect of strength or frequent lethal breakage would refute the claim; negligible effects in adequately powered samples would support it.

candidate_datasets.name: PANGAEA
candidate_datasets.role: Public sediment and assemblage records that may provide shell fragmentation and abundance proxies.

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: Occurrence histories for coarse tests of shell traits against persistence.

obstacles: Open datasets rarely link mechanical strength, breakage and fitness for the same populations.
Postmortem fragmentation is confounded with lethal damage.
Absence of an effect is difficult to establish.
assessments.rationale: The survival prediction is measurable, but existing public records mainly concern preserved shells rather than individual breakage hazards and fitness. A convincing causal test would require new mechanical and ecological measurements.

assessments.operationalization: Model foraminiferal shell abundance across sediment grain-size and current-speed gradients, including transport and settling traits, and compare hydraulic-sorting predictions with habitat-avoidance models based on living assemblages. Matching dead-shell distributions but different live distributions would support sorting; absence from both after flow controls would support avoidance.

candidate_datasets.name: PANGAEA
candidate_datasets.role: Open marine sediment, grain-size, current and foraminiferal assemblage datasets.

candidate_datasets.name: OBIS
candidate_datasets.role: Public marine species occurrences for comparing living distributions with sedimentary shells.

obstacles: Many assemblage datasets mix living and dead tests.
Dissolution and sampling gear also alter shell distributions.
assessments.rationale: The competing mechanisms make distinguishable predictions using paired biological and sedimentological observations. Large public marine repositories contain the needed variables, though harmonization and taphonomic controls are necessary.

assessments.operationalization: For traits with an independently supported physical generative model, quantify homoplasy by mapping form similarity onto molecular phylogenies. Excess similarity among distant relatives under shared physical regimes would show that form alone is unsafe evidence of kinship; close correspondence with independent trees would weaken the claim.

candidate_datasets.name: NCBI GenBank
candidate_datasets.role: Sequence data for phylogenies independent of morphology.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: Comparable 3D morphology for quantifying form similarity.

candidate_datasets.name: Open Tree of Life
candidate_datasets.role: Public synthetic phylogenies for broad comparative screening.

obstacles: The claim is conditional on first demonstrating physical control.
Taxonomic classification uses many characters, not form alone.
assessments.rationale: The warning has a clear empirical consequence—physically generated similarity should be homoplastic relative to independent trees. Data can test examples and estimate risk, but cannot settle the normative breadth of how classification 'must' be revised.

assessments.operationalization: Fit plane logarithmic and alternative curves to 3D rhinoceros horn centerlines and estimate anterior-posterior increment widths along growth rings. Constant differential-growth ratios coupled to stable spiral parameters would support the claim; lateral torsion, nonlogarithmic fit or changing ratios would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: Open 3D specimen media for horn centerline and surface measurements.

obstacles: Few digitized horns preserve measurable growth increments.
Museum sampling across ages and species is limited.
assessments.rationale: The shape and growth-ratio predictions are quantitative, but available public data are more likely to resolve geometry than the causal growth field. A targeted compilation could test selected species.

assessments.operationalization: Reflect one horn of each paired 3D specimen and quantify registration error against its mate, comparing observed symmetry with within-individual shape variation. Low residual asymmetry supports conjugate mirror-image spirals; systematic same-handedness or major nonmirror geometry refutes the claim.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: 3D bovid specimens for direct bilateral shape registration.

candidate_datasets.name: iDigBio
candidate_datasets.role: Aggregated public natural-history specimen records and images.

obstacles: Damage and pose differences can inflate asymmetry.
Some records show detached single horns rather than pairs.
assessments.rationale: Mirror symmetry has a direct, decisive geometric test requiring only paired specimens. Public museum media provide broad enough coverage to resolve the generalization for many bovid groups.

assessments.operationalization: Fit logarithmic and rival curves to horn centerlines across Bovidae and estimate opposite-side longitudinal increments from annuli where visible. Majority support requires stable logarithmic parameters and near-constant growth asymmetry through ontogeny; widespread better alternatives or ratio drift refutes it.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: Open 3D bovid skull and horn media for curve fitting.

candidate_datasets.name: iDigBio
candidate_datasets.role: Large public aggregation of specimen images and metadata.

obstacles: External geometry is much more available than side-specific growth increments.
The phrase 'great majority' requires representative taxonomic sampling.
assessments.rationale: The geometric majority claim can be tested now with public specimen media and standard curve model comparison. The specific constant-growth mechanism is only partially covered, but a strong geometric rejection would resolve the compound assertion.

assessments.operationalization: Fit species-specific logarithmic spiral angles to standardized horn centerlines for the named Oryx, Capra and Ovis taxa and test the stated ordering and approximate values. Nonlogarithmic fits, angles outside uncertainty bounds or a reversed ordering would refute the claim.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: 3D horn geometry for estimating spiral angles.

candidate_datasets.name: iDigBio
candidate_datasets.role: Additional digitized bovid specimens for within-species replication.

obstacles: Sex, age and subspecies can alter horn geometry.
Photographic perspective requires calibration or 3D records.
assessments.rationale: The named taxa, numerical angles and predicted ordering make this directly falsifiable. Public museum collections should provide enough specimens for a practical comparative test.

assessments.operationalization: Decompose 3D horn centerlines from Ovis ammon, O. poli and O. hodgsoni into planar logarithmic angle and out-of-plane helical components. Similar estimated spiral angles but significantly different torsion support the claim; substantial angle differences or similar torsion refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: 3D wild-sheep horn media for separating curvature and torsion.

candidate_datasets.name: iDigBio
candidate_datasets.role: Digitized museum specimens for taxonomic replication.

obstacles: Public 3D sample sizes for rare wild sheep may be small.
Taxonomic synonymy and specimen age require curation.
assessments.rationale: This is a clear comparison of two geometric parameters using standard 3D methods. Existing museum media likely suffice for a focused test, although population-level coverage may be limited.

assessments.operationalization: Measure circumferential growth-rate fields at the horn base through time and test whether diametrically opposed extrema predict zero torsion while offset extrema predict a helical component. The predicted relationship across developing horns would support the law; discordant growth fields and trajectories would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: Existing adult 3D geometry can characterize planar versus helical outcomes but not the required growth-rate field.

obstacles: Public collections provide final form, not spatially resolved growth velocities.
Longitudinal developmental imaging of horn growth appears necessary.
assessments.rationale: The prediction is mathematically operational, but its crucial independent variable is a developing basal growth field. Final horn shapes alone cannot establish where growth maxima and minima lay.

assessments.operationalization: Map sheath-core adhesion strength and local elongation around developing horn bases, then test whether spatially uneven adhesion predicts subsequent curvature independently of intrinsic growth. Experimental or longitudinal evidence that adhesion asymmetry alone generates the observed spiral would support the claim.
obstacles: No known open dataset links local sheath-core adhesion to subsequent horn geometry.
Intrinsic growth and mechanical retardation produce similar final forms.
The asserted importance requires comparative or perturbational evidence.
assessments.rationale: Adhesion and curvature can be defined, but adult museum morphology cannot discriminate adhesion-induced retardation from primary growth asymmetry. New developmental biomechanical data would be needed.

assessments.operationalization: Measure horn cross-sectional thickness and centerline curvature in a taxonomically broad 3D sample, then model their association with controls for body size, sex, age and phylogeny. A robust positive effect supports the claim; a null or negative effect with adequate power refutes it.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: 3D specimens for measuring horn thickness and curvature.

candidate_datasets.name: iDigBio
candidate_datasets.role: Public bovid specimen images and metadata to broaden taxonomic coverage.

candidate_datasets.name: Open Tree of Life
candidate_datasets.role: Phylogenetic relationships for comparative controls.

obstacles: Thickness and curvature both covary with body size and age.
External scans may not reveal sheath thickness separately from the core.
assessments.rationale: The comparative association is directly measurable with standard morphometrics. Public 3D collections can provide a substantial sample, though the proposed causal explanation is less directly tested.

assessments.operationalization: Quantify centerline torsion, cross-sectional eccentricity and growth-line sinuosity from high-resolution horn surfaces, and compare the observed warping with elastic-prism predictions. Covariation and correct predicted line orientation support the mechanism; sinuous rings without torsion or absent rings under high torsion refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: High-resolution 3D horn surfaces for measuring torsion and growth-line geometry.

obstacles: Surface resolution may be insufficient for growth rings.
Attachment forces and material properties are not recorded.
Weathering can mimic or erase sinuous lines.
assessments.rationale: Existing scans can test the predicted geometric association and elastic shape for selected specimens. Establishing torsional strain as the cause requires mechanical variables generally missing from public data.

assessments.operationalization: Analyze time-lapse stem growth to estimate side-specific elongation and test whether the moving growth asymmetry predicts circumvolution direction, phase and curvature. Correct temporal prediction supports the mechanism; twining without differential growth or phase mismatch refutes it.

candidate_datasets.name: BioStudies
candidate_datasets.role: Public study data and imaging supplements that may include plant time-lapse growth series.

candidate_datasets.name: Dryad
candidate_datasets.role: Open research datasets potentially containing stem kinematics and time-lapse measurements.

obstacles: Repository coverage of side-specific elongation is uncertain.
Twining species and growth conditions are heterogeneous.
assessments.rationale: Modern kinematics makes the mechanism directly testable, and some public time-lapse studies can address it. Existing coverage is unlikely to resolve the full scope of twining plants.

assessments.operationalization: Compare genetically and developmentally matched stems twining on supports differing only in calibrated roughness, measuring adhesion, torque and stem torsion over time. Torsion scaling with adhesion-generated torque supports the claim; equal torsion on smooth supports or no torque-torsion link refutes it.
obstacles: The required controlled rough-versus-smooth time series is not known as a reusable public dataset.
Support roughness also changes contact geometry and plant behavior.
assessments.rationale: The proposed mechanical couple yields a clean controlled test. Public observational plant records do not contain the force, adhesion and torsion measurements needed to distinguish it from adaptive or developmental alternatives.

assessments.operationalization: Fit a single smooth spheroid or ellipsoid to the 3D branch centerlines and tine tips of paired antlers, comparing residuals with separate surfaces and unconstrained branching models. Consistently small residuals and bilateral continuity support the claim; strongly noncoplanar or multi-surface arrangements refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: Open 3D cervid skull and antler models for surface fitting.

candidate_datasets.name: iDigBio
candidate_datasets.role: Aggregated public cervid specimen imagery and metadata.

obstacles: Damage and annual age affect tine completeness.
A tolerance for being 'confined' to one surface must be prespecified.
assessments.rationale: The assertion has a direct 3D geometric decision criterion. Public museum models and images should support a broad, feasible test across the named deer groups.

assessments.operationalization: Fit logarithmic, circular, polynomial and other spiral models to standardized centerlines of claws, beaks and ever-growing teeth across taxa, stratified by structure length. The claim requires logarithmic fits to predominate and become clearer with angular extent; systematic rival superiority refutes it.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: 3D vertebrate specimens containing beaks, claws and teeth for curve fitting.

obstacles: The universal word 'always' requires broad sampling.
Wear can substantially alter tooth and claw trajectories.
assessments.rationale: Logarithmic curvature is straightforward to test against explicit alternatives. Large public morphology collections make a strong cross-structure test feasible, although complete universality cannot be demonstrated.

assessments.operationalization: Fit scale-normalized logarithmic spiral parameters to complete tusk centerlines of living elephants, American mastodons and mammoths, and extrapolate shorter curves with uncertainty. Shared parameters support size-only difference; significant taxon-specific curvature or torsion refutes it.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: 3D proboscidean specimens for extracting tusk centerlines.

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: Fossil occurrence and taxonomy records for locating and contextualizing mastodon and mammoth specimens.

obstacles: Many fossil tusks are incomplete or deformed.
Sex, age and species produce substantial within-group variation.
assessments.rationale: The size-only and shared-spiral predictions are direct geometric hypotheses. Existing 3D fossil and museum resources permit model comparison across all named groups.

assessments.operationalization: Map organ positions on 3D surfaces from stems, cones and capitula, geometrically deform each surface to a common cylinder, and test whether the same indexed arrangement becomes helical while surface projections become logarithmic spirals. Topological and parameter continuity supports the claim; discontinuous rearrangement refutes it.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: 3D plant structures suitable for surface mapping where available.

candidate_datasets.name: iDigBio
candidate_datasets.role: Public specimen images of cones and inflorescences across taxa.

obstacles: Cross-taxon deformation does not itself establish developmental identity.
Open 3D coverage of intact inflorescences is limited.
assessments.rationale: The geometric equivalence can be tested computationally on digitized specimens. Existing data are adequate for examples but likely not for the full developmental assertion spanning all listed plant structures.

assessments.operationalization: Extract opposing parastichy families from calibrated sunflower images and measure their local intersection angles across each disc and among heads. Approximate constancy away from 90 degrees supports the claim; systematic angle variation or frequent orthogonality refutes it.

candidate_datasets.name: iDigBio
candidate_datasets.role: Open botanical specimen images including sunflower capitula.

candidate_datasets.name: Dryad
candidate_datasets.role: Open research datasets that may include high-resolution phyllotaxis imagery.

obstacles: Herbarium images may distort three-dimensional capitula.
Parastichy tracing can be ambiguous near the disc center and edge.
assessments.rationale: Intersection angles are directly measurable and sharply distinguish isogonal from orthogonal patterns. Large public image sources and straightforward image analysis make the prediction resolvable now.

assessments.operationalization: Use time-lapse meristem datasets to quantify initiation intervals, organ similarity and placement, then test whether these inputs alone predict subsequent helical or spiral arrangements. Accurate out-of-sample prediction supports sufficiency; systematic need for additional interactions refutes the 'necessarily' claim.

candidate_datasets.name: BioStudies
candidate_datasets.role: Public imaging studies that may include developmental meristem time series.

candidate_datasets.name: Dryad
candidate_datasets.role: Open plant-development datasets and supplementary measurements.

obstacles: 'Similarly placed' risks defining the resulting pattern circularly.
Time-resolved organ initiation datasets cover few species.
Mechanical and inhibitory interactions are plausible hidden variables.
assessments.rationale: A predictive developmental model can test a restricted sufficiency claim. Thompson's broad language is partly circular and existing time-lapse data have narrow taxonomic coverage.

assessments.operationalization: Count opposing parastichy families in many georeferenced cones per conifer species and estimate within-species frequency distributions, explicitly checking the stated 5/3 spruce and 8/5 larch modes. Tight species-specific modes support the claim; broad variation or different dominant counts refutes it.

candidate_datasets.name: iDigBio
candidate_datasets.role: Aggregated natural-history specimen images of conifer cones.

obstacles: Images must show the cone at sufficient resolution and orientation.
Cultivar, age and cone position may contribute within-species variation.
assessments.rationale: Counts and species identity are direct variables, and public specimen imagery can yield large samples. The named examples and constancy criterion provide clear confirming and refuting outcomes.

assessments.operationalization: Measure capitulum diameter and parastichy count pairs across sunflower heads within and among species, then model count transitions with size while controlling developmental stage. Positive, ordered transitions such as 34/55 to 55/89 to 89/144 support the claim; size-independent counts refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: iDigBio
candidate_datasets.role: Public sunflower specimen images for disc size and parastichy counts.

candidate_datasets.name: Dryad
candidate_datasets.role: Open phenotyping datasets that may contain sunflower head images and dimensions.

obstacles: Size and developmental stage are correlated.
Very dense high-order spirals require high-resolution images.
assessments.rationale: Both disc size and row counts can be extracted from existing images with standard methods. Adequate within-species replication can directly test the predicted association and listed transitions.

assessments.operationalization: Score handedness of a designated parastichy family in large species-stratified cone image samples and test frequencies against 0.5, including a replication of the Norway spruce 5/8 class. Strong balanced frequencies support the claim; consistent directional bias refutes it.

candidate_datasets.name: iDigBio
candidate_datasets.role: Large public collection of conifer cone images.

obstacles: A consistent viewing convention is needed to assign handedness.
Image availability may be spatially and taxonomically biased.
assessments.rationale: This is a simple binomial prediction with an explicit historical benchmark. Public cone imagery should provide sufficient sample size for a decisive modern test.

assessments.operationalization: Reconstruct the indexed genetic spiral from high-resolution organ maps, enumerate every parastichy family, and test whether observation of a higher Fibonacci pair always co-occurs with all lower pairs under one prespecified visibility-independent definition. A single valid counterexample refutes necessity; universal co-occurrence in broad data supports it.

candidate_datasets.name: iDigBio
candidate_datasets.role: Public high-resolution cone and inflorescence images for organ indexing.

candidate_datasets.name: Dryad
candidate_datasets.role: Open quantitative phyllotaxis datasets and image supplements.

obstacles: Implicit mathematical parastichies must be distinguished from visually conspicuous ones.
Occlusion can hide lower-order connections.
assessments.rationale: The necessity statement is a crisp combinatorial prediction once the genetic spiral is indexed. Existing images can supply many tests, and model-based enumeration avoids relying only on visual prominence.

assessments.operationalization: Infer the number of organs per turn of the genetic spiral from indexed cone and inflorescence images and estimate the fraction lying between two and three, along with frequencies corresponding to t = 3, 4 and 5. A clear majority in the stated interval supports the claim; another interval dominating refutes it.

candidate_datasets.name: iDigBio
candidate_datasets.role: Digitized cones and plant structures for reconstructing organ sequences.

candidate_datasets.name: Dryad
candidate_datasets.role: Open phyllotaxis research data for higher-resolution validation.

obstacles: The genetic order is often not recoverable from a single mature image.
Available imagery is not representative of all phyllotactic systems.
assessments.rationale: The numerical prevalence claim is measurable, but genetic-spiral reconstruction requires high-quality organ maps. Current data can test fir-cones and selected taxa, not confidently the claimed host of systems.

assessments.operationalization: For organ maps with measured divergence, leaf-area rhomboid diagonals and observer-independent prominence scores, regress which parastichy family is conspicuous on shape ratio versus divergence. Dominance by diagonal ratio after controlling divergence supports the claim; a strong independent divergence effect refutes it.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: 3D plant morphology where organ proportions and arrangements can be jointly measured.

candidate_datasets.name: Dryad
candidate_datasets.role: Open phyllotaxis imaging datasets potentially containing the required organ maps.

obstacles: Conspicuousness needs a reproducible visual or image-processing definition.
Few public datasets jointly measure divergence and individual organ proportions.
Shape and divergence may covary developmentally.
assessments.rationale: The two rival predictors permit a strong statistical comparison. However, the joint measurements needed are uncommon and likely support only selected systems without new annotation.

assessments.operationalization: The mathematical convergence is demonstrable, but 'no biological significance' has no unique measurable consequence without specifying a biological function or causal model. Particular hypotheses, such as improved packing or light interception near the golden angle, can be tested, but no finite dataset can exclude every significance.
obstacles: Biological significance is undefined and ranges over unlimited possible functions.
The exact numerical convergence is a mathematical fact rather than an empirical claim.
assessments.rationale: Existing plant data can refute or support specific adaptive explanations, but Thompson's unrestricted absence claim is not operationally bounded. Any observed pattern can be redescribed without settling whether it is 'significant.'

assessments.operationalization: Compile divergence fractions or parastichy ratios from a taxonomically stratified plant sample and compare prevalence of the listed close and poor approximations. Higher frequencies of 1/2, 2/3 and 3/5 than 8/13 and above support the claim; opposite frequencies refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: iDigBio
candidate_datasets.role: Public specimen imagery from which phyllotactic ratios can be scored.

candidate_datasets.name: TRY Plant Trait Database
candidate_datasets.role: Plant trait resource that can support taxonomic and trait-based sampling, subject to dataset access terms.

obstacles: Image-based samples overrepresent large, conspicuous reproductive structures.
Ratios are not routinely encoded and require extensive annotation.
assessments.rationale: Frequency categories and outcomes are explicit, and a substantial test can be built from existing images. Resolving the assertion across plants would require a large harmonized survey not currently available as a direct table.

assessments.operationalization: Use 3D shoot architectures and radiative-transfer or airflow models to independently vary internode length and divergence angle, measuring marginal changes in light and air exposure. A consistently larger effect of internode elongation supports the prediction; equal or larger divergence effects refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: 3D plant architectures where available for counterfactual geometric modeling.

candidate_datasets.name: Dryad
candidate_datasets.role: Open plant architecture and functional-trait datasets for selected species.

obstacles: Model results depend on canopy, sun angle, leaf posture and the definition of exposure.
Open 3D shoot datasets cover few species.
Internode length has costs and functions omitted from the comparison.
assessments.rationale: The comparative effect can be quantified under explicit physical conditions, but Thompson leaves exposure and biological context underspecified. Existing architectures permit restricted simulation tests rather than a universal conclusion.

assessments.operationalization: Specific adaptive hypotheses could relate Fibonacci phyllotaxis to measured fitness components and compare them with developmental null models, but the assertion that these ideas deserve 'no place' is normative. No dataset can directly decide that disciplinary prescription or exclude every possible adaptive role.
obstacles: The conclusion is normative rather than a bounded empirical prediction.
Natural selection's historical contribution is difficult to separate from developmental constraints using extant correlations.
assessments.rationale: Parts of the premise, such as packing or light-interception benefits, are testable under specified models. The claim as stated combines a universal absence of adaptive role with a judgment about scientific relevance, so it is not empirically resolvable.

assessments.operationalization: Compute principal-axis ratios and rotational asymmetry from large image or 3D samples of bird, tortoise and crocodile eggs, classifying prolate, oblate and non-axisymmetric forms with preset thresholds. Any credible oblate or discoidal hard-shelled egg refutes the absolute claim; consistently prolate samples support it.

candidate_datasets.name: iDigBio
candidate_datasets.role: Aggregated museum egg images across birds and reptiles.

obstacles: Two-dimensional images can misclassify non-axisymmetric eggs.
Museum egg collections have taxonomic and collecting biases.
assessments.rationale: Shape class is directly measurable, and the universal assertion is vulnerable to clear counterexamples. Extensive public museum imagery makes a broad and decisive test feasible.

assessments.operationalization: Across bird species, relate quantitative egg asymmetry and posterior taper to egg volume divided by adult female body size, controlling phylogeny and ecology. A robust positive association supports the empirical rule; no association refutes it, while direct oviduct dimensions would be needed for the pressure explanation.

candidate_datasets.name: iDigBio
candidate_datasets.role: Public egg specimen images and taxonomic metadata.

candidate_datasets.name: Amniote Life-History Database
candidate_datasets.role: Public species-level body mass and reproductive trait data for relative egg-size calculations.

obstacles: Oviduct size and in vivo pressure are generally absent.
Phylogeny, flight ecology and clutch strategy confound the association.
assessments.rationale: The cross-species empirical relationship can be tested well with public egg and body-size data. The mechanistic explanation by oviduct pressure is only indirectly discriminated, but the central 'common rule' is resolvable.

assessments.operationalization: Analyze hen-level longitudinal laying records with egg mass and shape index, testing whether first eggs are smaller and rounder than later eggs and whether breeds with smaller relative eggs have rounder shapes. Consistent within-hen trajectories and breed effects support the claim; absent or reversed effects refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: Ag Data Commons
candidate_datasets.role: Public agricultural research datasets that may include poultry egg production and quality measurements.

candidate_datasets.name: Dryad
candidate_datasets.role: Open animal-science datasets potentially containing repeated egg measurements.

obstacles: Public poultry datasets often omit egg shape or exact laying order.
Feed, age, housing and selection line confound breed comparisons.
assessments.rationale: The within-individual prediction is direct and highly discriminating. Existing public records likely test subsets, but a dataset jointly containing laying sequence, size and shape across breeds is not assured.

assessments.operationalization: Synchronize in vivo oviduct pressure maps and peristaltic-wave direction with repeated imaging of the deformable egg, then test whether peak pressure lies posterior to mid-egg and predicts anterior broadening, posterior taper and blunt-end-first transport. Mismatched pressure location or transport orientation would refute the mechanism.
obstacles: Public egg-shape datasets do not include spatial pressure during shell formation.
Direct oviduct imaging and manometry are specialized and invasive.
Final shape alone cannot localize the causal pressure maximum.
assessments.rationale: The mechanism makes measurable temporal predictions, but the decisive physiological variables are absent from standard repositories. Existing morphology cannot distinguish peristaltic pressure from other developmental causes.

assessments.operationalization: Measure ring-by-ring oviduct pressure and egg deformation before calcification across species and experimentally model whether those pressures predict final shape better than nesting ecology and intrinsic membrane properties. Accurate pressure-based prediction and weak independent nesting effects support the claim; the reverse refutes it.
obstacles: No known public dataset contains pre-shell pressure fields linked to final egg form.
Pressure, membrane mechanics and secretion are jointly determined.
The claim's 'essential cause' requires causal comparison with ecological alternatives.
assessments.rationale: The proposed cause is testable in principle but not from existing egg image and trait databases. New longitudinal physiological and mechanical measurements are required for discrimination.

assessments.operationalization: For eggs sampled before shell hardening, jointly measure local principal curvatures, external normal pressure, membrane tension and internal pressure, then test pointwise closure of the equation and compare residuals with richer anisotropic-shell models. Systematic nonzero residuals beyond measurement error would refute the asserted law.
obstacles: Public datasets lack co-registered membrane tension and pressure fields.
Hard shells violate the extensible-membrane postulate.
Material anisotropy and spatially varying thickness are plausible omitted terms.
assessments.rationale: The equation is explicit and falsifiable, but shape alone leaves too many unknown fields to test it. Existing museum geometry cannot provide a noncircular estimate of all terms.

assessments.operationalization: Code the spatial location of cracks, distortions and shape abnormalities on pointed eggs and compare their frequency near the small versus large end, while using shell mechanics to infer tension. Concentration at the small end supports the prediction; uniform or opposite localization refutes it.

candidate_datasets.name: iDigBio
candidate_datasets.role: Aggregated egg collection images for enlarging the abnormal-specimen sample.

candidate_datasets.name: Ag Data Commons
candidate_datasets.role: Public poultry quality data that may include shell defects and breakage.

obstacles: Collections may exclude broken or abnormal eggs.
Damage after laying can mimic developmental failure.
Abnormality location tests the consequence, not tension directly.
assessments.rationale: The predicted localization can be tested on existing images and production records, though ascertainment bias is serious. Direct confirmation of maximum membrane tension would require new mechanical measurements.

assessments.operationalization: Link egg spine position to independently identified adult worms using morphology and genomic sequences, and test whether lateral- and terminal-spined eggs occur within one reproducing lineage or segregate into distinct lineages. Stable genomic separation supports separate species and refutes Thompson; within-lineage mechanical switching would support his claim.

candidate_datasets.name: WormBase ParaSite
candidate_datasets.role: Public Schistosoma genomes, comparative genomics and species resources.

candidate_datasets.name: NCBI GenBank
candidate_datasets.role: Public Schistosoma sequence records for independent species delimitation.

candidate_datasets.name: WHO Schistosomiasis Data
candidate_datasets.role: Public epidemiological context for distributions of recognized Schistosoma species.

obstacles: Historical egg images may not be linked to sequenced adult worms.
Hybridization can complicate species boundaries.
Public data test species distinctness more directly than ootype moulding.
assessments.rationale: The assertion that S. mansoni is not a separate species has a decisive test using abundant modern genomic data. The specific funnel-moulding mechanism is less well covered, but the compound claim can be clearly refuted or supported at its principal taxonomic consequence.

assessments.operationalization: Fit axisymmetric capillary-drop models to 3D echinoid tests and test whether flattening covaries with shell stiffness and tube-foot loading. Systematic residuals or absent stiffness-shape covariation would refute the stated account.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: Public 3D echinoid test scans for outline and curvature measurements.

obstacles: Shell stiffness and tube-foot force are rarely paired with scans.
Preserved tests omit living soft-tissue loading.
assessments.rationale: Shape is directly measurable and the drop model gives quantitative predictions. Public scans support a taxonomically restricted shape test, but paired mechanical variables are sparse, so the full causal claim is only partly resolvable.

assessments.operationalization: Measure lumen radius, wall thickness and pressure along arterial trees and fit the predicted large-vessel proportionality and small-vessel downward deviation. Models with and without pressure decline can be compared.

candidate_datasets.name: Vascular Model Repository
candidate_datasets.role: Open vascular geometries for radius and wall-related morphometry.

candidate_datasets.name: PhysioNet
candidate_datasets.role: Public physiological waveforms and pressure records for complementary hemodynamic estimates.

obstacles: Geometry and local pressure are generally not measured in the same subjects.
Capillary wall thickness requires histology or microscopy.
assessments.rationale: The scaling relation and deviation are explicit. Relevant open measurements exist, but joining vessel-scale anatomy to local pressure across the complete arterial-capillary range requires heterogeneous sources.

assessments.operationalization: From segmented cardiac images, calculate local principal curvatures and wall thickness within each chamber, then test whether thickness times mean curvature is constant and whether the apex is thinnest.

candidate_datasets.name: Cardiac Atlas Project
candidate_datasets.role: Public cardiac imaging resources and shape models for chamber geometry.

candidate_datasets.name: The Cancer Imaging Archive
candidate_datasets.role: Open CT and MR collections that include cardiac anatomy.

obstacles: Wall thickness varies with cardiac phase and loading.
Most open cohorts emphasize humans rather than mammals broadly.
assessments.rationale: The equation maps cleanly to imaging variables and can be tested with standard segmentation and surface analysis. Existing data permit a strong human test but do not match the full mammalian scope or uniform-pressure assumption.

assessments.operationalization: Estimate left:right ventricular systolic pressure and matched wall-thickness ratios in mammalian hearts. Ratios near six to seven in both measures support the claim; discordant or systematically different ratios refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: Cardiac Atlas Project
candidate_datasets.role: Cardiac images and models for ventricular wall measurements.

candidate_datasets.name: PhysioNet
candidate_datasets.role: Open pressure and cardiovascular records for estimating chamber pressure ratios.

obstacles: Matched invasive pressures and images are uncommon.
Species and disease state strongly affect ratios.
assessments.rationale: Both quantities and the numerical criterion are unambiguous. Public human data can test important portions, but matched records and broad healthy mammalian coverage are limited.

assessments.operationalization: Reconstruct vascular networks, calculate pumping-power and wall-area costs, and compare observed networks with constrained alternative branching networks. Closeness to a Pareto optimum would support, while feasible networks dominating both costs would refute, the claim.

candidate_datasets.name: Vascular Model Repository
candidate_datasets.role: Open vascular geometries for network cost calculations.

candidate_datasets.name: BioImage Archive
candidate_datasets.role: Public microscopy datasets that can include vascular networks.

obstacles: “Minimum” depends on unspecified anatomical and functional constraints.
Most datasets capture only part of a vascular tree.
assessments.rationale: Optimization can be formulated, but the intended constraint set and trade-off between effort and surface are underdetermined. Open networks permit restricted tests rather than a decisive vertebrate-wide result.

assessments.operationalization: Measure parent and daughter diameters and branch angles in segmented arterial trees, then regress angle on relative branch caliber and test symmetry for equal daughters. A flat or reversed relationship would refute the rule.

candidate_datasets.name: Vascular Model Repository
candidate_datasets.role: Segmented vessel geometries for caliber and angle measurements.

candidate_datasets.name: The Cancer Imaging Archive
candidate_datasets.role: Open angiographic CT and MR images for additional arterial trees.

obstacles: Clinical scans favor large vessels.
Branch angle depends on organ, flow state and imaging posture.
assessments.rationale: The variables and directional prediction are direct and standard geometric analyses are feasible. Coverage of the smallest branches and vertebrate diversity is insufficient for the universal scope.

assessments.operationalization: For each bifurcation, estimate energy loss per unit length in trunk and branch from matched geometry and flow, and compare observed angle with arccos(L/L′). Persistent deviations beyond measurement error would refute the law.

candidate_datasets.name: Vascular Model Repository
candidate_datasets.role: Vessel geometries and some flow models for partial evaluation.

obstacles: Matched local energy losses and branch angles are rarely available.
Pulsatile non-Newtonian flow complicates L and L′.
assessments.rationale: The equation is explicit and discriminating. Geometry is public, but the branch-resolved in vivo flow and loss measurements needed across vertebrate arteries are generally absent, making a direct test data-limited.

assessments.operationalization: Define demonstrability as out-of-sample predictive performance of mechanical morphology models versus coloration-function models across species, and compare effect sizes and uncertainty. This tests the contrast, though not the philosophical assertion in full.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: Open animal morphology for mechanical performance models.

obstacles: “Can be demonstrated” is epistemic rather than a single biological variable.
Evidence quality differs for reasons unrelated to inherent testability.
assessments.rationale: Mechanical efficiency is empirically measurable, but the categorical contrast with all cryptic, warning and mimetic explanations needs substantial reinterpretation. Existing data can compare selected cases only.

assessments.operationalization: Compile matched tensile and compressive ultimate strengths of fresh bone by species, element and orientation, then test whether their ratio is near one and within the stated ranges.

candidate_datasets.name: Dryad
candidate_datasets.role: Open research datasets that include biomechanical tests of bone.

obstacles: Fresh-bone paired tests are scattered.
Strength depends strongly on orientation, hydration, age and strain rate.
assessments.rationale: The claim gives standard variables and numerical ranges, so contrary data would clearly refute it. Public records exist but are heterogeneous and do not adequately cover living vertebrate bone generally.

assessments.operationalization: Quantify cross-sectional hollowness and second moment of area in structures exposed to multidirectional bending, comparing them with structures under other dominant loads while controlling size. Frequent solid cores in the target class would refute the generalization.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: 3D and CT scans of vertebrate bones for cross-sectional geometry.

candidate_datasets.name: BioImage Archive
candidate_datasets.role: Open biological images including plant and feather microstructure.

obstacles: Loading regime is not encoded with most scans.
The scope combines nonhomologous animal and plant structures.
assessments.rationale: Hollowness and bending efficiency are measurable, but “where required” risks selecting cases by the outcome. Open scans support broad comparative tests, though functional loading and full taxonomic coverage remain incomplete.

assessments.operationalization: Extract cortical wall thickness along CT-scanned femora and compare its longitudinal profile with bending moments from musculoskeletal or beam models. Correlation after accounting for axial and torsional loads supports the claim.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: CT scans of long bones for longitudinal cortical measurements.

candidate_datasets.name: The Cancer Imaging Archive
candidate_datasets.role: Open human CT collections for femoral geometry.

obstacles: Muscle forces and habitual loading are usually not paired with bone scans.
Epiphyses and shaft are subject to multiple load modes.
assessments.rationale: The predicted profile is quantitative and scan analysis is straightforward. Available imaging can test humans and selected taxa, but estimating subject-specific bending moments and covering weight-bearing bones broadly limits resolution.

assessments.operationalization: Estimate trabecular fabric tensors from micro-CT and principal stress directions from finite-element models under physiological loads, then test alignment and orthogonal crossing. Random or consistently oblique architecture would refute the claim.

candidate_datasets.name: Digital Morphology
candidate_datasets.role: Public high-resolution CT scans of vertebrate skeletal material.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: CT datasets for trabecular architecture across taxa.

obstacles: Resolution is inadequate in many whole-bone scans.
Stress estimates depend on uncertain boundary and muscle loads.
assessments.rationale: Modern fabric analysis and finite elements map well to the statement. Open micro-CT can test selected bones and species, but paired loading information and broad coverage are limited, and several loading histories can yield similar fabric.

assessments.operationalization: Track individual trabeculae longitudinally under known loading and test whether oblique elements experience greater shear and are displaced or resorbed toward principal stress directions while aligned elements persist.

candidate_datasets.name: BioImage Archive
candidate_datasets.role: Potential public longitudinal microscopy and micro-CT image series for bone remodeling.

obstacles: Individual-trabecula longitudinal imaging under measured loads is rare.
Remodeling by resorption and formation is not literal mechanical displacement.
assessments.rationale: The mechanism has measurable consequences but Thompson's “move” requires interpretive mapping to remodeling. Static scans cannot distinguish shear-driven selection from biological mechanosensing alternatives; decisive longitudinal paired data are lacking.

assessments.operationalization: Use serial CT after malunited fracture to quantify changes in trabecular orientation locally and distally, comparing them with changing finite-element principal stresses and uninjured controls. Complete alignment within weeks is the stated criterion.

candidate_datasets.name: The Cancer Imaging Archive
candidate_datasets.role: Open longitudinal clinical imaging, potentially including fracture follow-up.

obstacles: Public serial high-resolution scans of malunion are scarce.
Clinical CT seldom resolves trabeculae adequately.
The weeks-scale and “entirely remodelled” criteria are demanding.
assessments.rationale: The prediction is specific, temporal and highly testable in principle. Existing repositories do not provide enough serial microarchitecture plus loading data to resolve it, especially away from the injury.

assessments.operationalization: Relate experimentally or naturally increased mechanical strain to subsequent tissue growth or thickening using longitudinal controls and dose-response models. Growth without increased strain, or strain without subsequent growth under viable conditions, would challenge the direct mechanism.

candidate_datasets.name: Dryad
candidate_datasets.role: Open datasets from bone, plant and tissue loading experiments.

candidate_datasets.name: BioStudies
candidate_datasets.role: Public study data that can include mechanobiology experiments.

obstacles: Load, strain and growth are rarely all measured.
Hormonal and injury responses confound direct causation.
The scope spans very different tissues and kingdoms.
assessments.rationale: Mechanobiological response is measurable, but “direct stimulus” requires causal data and a modern interpretation. Existing experimental datasets test subsets such as bone, while the universal tissue claim remains inadequately covered.

assessments.operationalization: Build musculoskeletal free-body models of standing quadrupeds and compare force transmission and horizontal thrust under arch, tied-arch and double-cantilever idealizations. The model class that uniquely matches measured reactions and ligament strains provides the test.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: Vertebral and whole-skeleton geometry for structural models.

candidate_datasets.name: Movebank
candidate_datasets.role: Public animal movement data for posture and locomotor context.

assessments.operationalization: Measure neural-spine height along reconstructed vertebral columns, calculate local bending moments for standardized postures, and test proportionality within and across species. Alternative models based on muscle leverage should be compared.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: 3D vertebral scans and skeletons for spine-height profiles.

candidate_datasets.name: Digital Morphology
candidate_datasets.role: Public CT morphology of vertebrates.

obstacles: Moment profiles require uncertain body-mass and muscle-force estimates.
