assessments.operationalization: In segmented cell aggregates, compare wall areas and junction angles with the minimal-area surfaces expected for the observed cell volumes. Agreement with minimal-area geometry would support the geometric half; systematic excess area or a different angle rule would refute it, while an independent tension measurement would be required to credit surface tension rather than another minimizing agency.

candidate_datasets.name: Arabidopsis shoot-meristem segmentations
candidate_datasets.role: Open 3D confocal stacks and expert segmentations of shoot apical meristems for junction angles and cell-face areas

candidate_datasets.name: Arabidopsis embryo image collection
candidate_datasets.role: About 100 confocal volumes of early embryos with cell walls stained, for aggregate geometry from the one-cell stage onward

obstacles: Minimal-area packing is also predicted by adhesion energy and cortical contractility, which these images do not separate from surface tension.
Plant meristems and a few animal epithelia stand in for tissues in general.
assessments.rationale: Segmented tissues already in public archives are enough to test whether cell aggregates approximate surfaces of relatively minimal area. That is the measurable pattern the claim predicts. Naming surface tension as the agency needs a force measurement these datasets do not contain, so the geometric half is testable and the causal half remains confounded.

assessments.operationalization: Classify plant-cell junctions by whether the older wall was already rigid when the new partition met it, and measure the angle. Right angles confined to rigid-wall meetings, with fluid-fluid meetings near 120 degrees, would support the claim; right angles between walls that were still fluid, or 120-degree meetings against already rigid walls, would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: Arabidopsis shoot-meristem segmentations
candidate_datasets.role: Time-resolved meristem volumes from which successive walls and their meeting angles can be measured

candidate_datasets.name: Arabidopsis embryo image collection
candidate_datasets.role: Fixed embryo volumes spanning successive divisions, for angle statistics where wall age can be inferred from the lineage

obstacles: Wall rigidity is usually inferred from age or cellulose signal rather than measured directly in these stacks.
Coverage is concentrated on Arabidopsis, not plant tissues at large.
assessments.rationale: The angle prediction is sharp, and meristem and embryo volumes contain the walls. What they lack for a full test is a direct marker that the older wall had solidified before the new one arrived. Angle-versus-sequence comparisons are feasible for Arabidopsis and remain a proxy for the rigidity mechanism across plants.

assessments.operationalization: In filamentous cyanobacteria and similar pairs, class partition curvature as flat, hemispheric or more than hemispheric and, where possible, compare that class with measured tension at the outer surface and at the cell-cell boundary. The three shape classes tracking the three tension regimes would support the claim; shapes that stay flat across independently varied boundary tension would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: BioImage Archive
candidate_datasets.role: Public micrographs of filamentous and paired cells from which partition curvature can be scored

candidate_datasets.name: Cell Image Library
candidate_datasets.role: Additional annotated light and electron micrographs of simple cell chains

obstacles: Under a soap-film model the curvature is the tension ratio, so shape classes alone restate the claim.
Independent tension measurements in Nostoc and its allies are not part of these image archives.
assessments.rationale: Photographs can sort paired cells into the three curvature classes the claim names. They cannot supply the two tensions those classes are said to express, and treating curvature as a tension measurement makes the test circular. The shape catalogue is therefore only a partial check.

assessments.operationalization: In three-dimensional segmentations of parenchyma, epithelia and early embryos, measure the angles at which walls meet and the curvature of walls between cells of different sizes. Triple junctions near 120 degrees regardless of cell size, with curvature set by the size difference, would support the claim; common four-way junctions, angles far from 120 degrees, or curvature unrelated to neighbouring sizes would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: Arabidopsis shoot-meristem segmentations
candidate_datasets.role: Expert 3D segmentations of meristem cells for triple-junction angles and neighbour-size effects on wall curvature

candidate_datasets.name: Arabidopsis embryo image collection
candidate_datasets.role: Cell-wall-stained embryo volumes spanning many cell sizes in one aggregate

obstacles: Anisotropic stress and recent divisions are known to pull some junctions off 120 degrees, so the test needs a pre-registered exclusion or a report of that bias.
Honeycomb and every plant parenchyma type are not in these three collections.
assessments.rationale: Triple-junction angle and wall curvature are standard measurements on segmentations that can already be downloaded. The prediction that angle is independent of cell size while curvature is not is distinguishable from right-angle or random-junction alternatives. A small team can run that test on meristems, embryos and public epithelia with existing tools.

assessments.operationalization: In four-cell embryos whose blastomeres are in full contact, score whether a polar furrow is present or the four cells meet at one point. A short intermediate partition in essentially every such embryo would support the claim; stable four-way crosses in fully apposed fluid blastomeres would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: SSBD
candidate_datasets.role: Downloadable embryo image and quantitative-dynamics sets for remeasuring four-cell contacts in three dimensions

obstacles: A cross seen in a single optical plane can hide a short polar furrow, so only 3D or time-resolved volumes are decisive.
Molluscs and annelids, classical material for this stage, are less completely archived than frog and sea urchin.
assessments.rationale: Presence or absence of a polar furrow is a yes-or-no observation, and public cleavage images of frog, sea urchin and other embryos are sufficient to make it. Three-dimensional sets remove the viewing-angle error the claim says produced reports of a simple cross. Coverage is uneven across phyla, but it is enough to confirm or refute the pattern in eggs whose blastomeres meet in full contact.

assessments.operationalization: Measure the external contact angle of neighbouring blastomeres and, separately, the tensions at cell-cell and cell-medium surfaces. External angles below 120 degrees where cell-cell tension exceeds either cell-medium tension, and point contact where cell-cell tension reaches the sum of the other two, would support the claim.

candidate_datasets.name: SSBD
candidate_datasets.role: Quantitative embryo image sets from which contact angles and intercellular spaces can be measured

obstacles: Contact angle defines the tension ratio if Young's law is assumed, so geometry alone does not independently test the tensions.
Eggshells and extracellular coats can hold blastomeres apart and mimic point contact.
assessments.rationale: Rounded blastomeres and the angles of their contacts are measurable in existing embryo volumes. The claim's content is a tension inequality, and these archives do not contain the tensions. The geometric catalogue can be checked, while the force law remains confounded with extracellular constraints.

assessments.operationalization: Compare outer-layer cells with interior cells for flattening, rectangular outline and near-right angles at the outer wall, and ask whether those traits track position alone. Outer cells showing that suite because they lie outside, including after identity programs are perturbed, would support the claim; an epidermal shape program that appears independent of outside position would limit it.

candidate_datasets.name: Arabidopsis embryo image collection
candidate_datasets.role: Early embryo volumes in which the outer cell layer can be compared with interior cells

candidate_datasets.name: Arabidopsis shoot-meristem segmentations
candidate_datasets.role: Segmented meristems with an outer layer whose angles and aspect ratios are measurable

obstacles: Position and epidermal identity are usually confounded, and these geometry sets do not include the identity-perturbation experiments.
Laminaria-type simple thalli are not in the Arabidopsis-heavy archives.
assessments.rationale: Outer versus inner cell shape is directly measurable in open embryo and meristem segmentations, so the positional pattern can be tested. The claim also says the physical features follow from that position through unequal, consolidated tensions, which the images do not measure. Identity programs remain a live alternative for the same flattened outer layer.

assessments.operationalization: Relate polygon regularity, such as variation in side length and angle, to cell-size variation and to directional stretch in surface epithelia and parenchyma. Regular hexagons restricted to regions of uniform cell size and no directional traction, with irregular or elongated polygons where size varies or growth is anisotropic, would support the claim.

candidate_datasets.name: Arabidopsis shoot-meristem segmentations
candidate_datasets.role: Segmented meristem surfaces where cell-size variation and polygon regularity can be compared locally

candidate_datasets.name: Honeycomb X-ray microscopy
candidate_datasets.role: Three-dimensional comb reconstructions of similar-sized hexagonal cells as a uniform-size comparison

obstacles: Retinal pigment epithelium, Thompson's showcase of regular hexagons, is not a tabulated layer in these sets and would have to be added from other public images.
Average side number near six is expected from topology alone, so the test has to use regularity, not merely the mean.
assessments.rationale: Regularity against cell-size variation is a direct morphometric comparison, and segmented meristems already contain both variables, including local contrasts between equal and unequal cells. Epithelial volumes and uniform comb cells extend the comparison. The named retinal epithelium is a gap in coverage, not a gap in method, and the outcome would still favour or count against the stated size rule.

assessments.operationalization: Wherever similar cylinders or spheres are in complete surface contact, measure neighbour number and junction angle in section or surface view, and compare them with loose bundles that do not touch along faces. Complete contact yielding hexagons with angles near 120 degrees, and incomplete contact leaving round profiles, would support the claim.

candidate_datasets.name: Arabidopsis shoot-meristem segmentations
candidate_datasets.role: Close-packed meristem cells for neighbour counts and junction angles

candidate_datasets.name: Honeycomb X-ray microscopy
candidate_datasets.role: Three-dimensional bee comb, a close-packed hexagonal prism system in the claim's scope

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: Public 3D scans of colonial corals and other packed biological bodies for contact versus cylindrical outlines

obstacles: Any trivalent tiling averages six sides, so neighbour number alone is a weak discriminator and angle plus completeness of contact have to carry the test.
Scans and segmentations over-represent model plants, honeybees and a few coral colonies.
assessments.rationale: The packing prediction can be scored with neighbour counts and angles on data that already exist for epithelia, comb and corals. The informative contrast is complete facial contact versus cylinders that only touch locally. That comparison is standard image analysis and is sufficient to confirm or refute the stated tendency, with the topological average kept in view as a bias.

assessments.operationalization: Count corallite sides in massive colonies whose polyps are in contact and compare the mean and the spread with fasciculate colonies whose corallites stay free. Close-packed colonies with a mean near six sides, more spread where sizes vary, and cylindrical corallites where contact is loose, would support the claim.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: Downloadable 3D scans of colonial coral skeletons from which corallite outlines and contacts can be counted

candidate_datasets.name: iDigBio
candidate_datasets.role: Aggregated museum images of fossil and living corals, including massive and fasciculate colony forms

candidate_datasets.name: Coral Trait Database
candidate_datasets.role: Open trait tables of colony growth form and calyx morphology for separating close-packed from loosely branched species

obstacles: Side number is not a column in the trait database and has to be counted from images and scans.
Paleozoic genera named by Thompson are photographed less evenly than living massive corals, and abrasion can round corners.
assessments.rationale: Mean side number under close contact, versus cylindrical outlines when corallites are free, is a direct count on public specimen images and scans. Colony growth form is already tabulated and sorts the two habits. Counting a broad sample is weeks of ordinary morphometry, enough to resolve the packing claim for massive versus fasciculate colonies.

assessments.operationalization: On three-dimensional reconstructions of hive-bee comb, measure the prism angles in plan and the angles of the three rhombs that close the cell. Prism angles near 120 degrees and a trihedral angle near 109.5 degrees would support the rhombic-dodecahedron description; a flat or differently angled base would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: Honeycomb X-ray microscopy
candidate_datasets.role: X-ray volumes and reconstructions of Apis mellifera comb from which prism and, where the base is in frame, rhomb angles can be measured

candidate_datasets.name: Natural comb cell-orientation measurements
candidate_datasets.role: Measured in-plane orientations of hexagonal cells in natural Apis mellifera and Apis cerana combs

obstacles: The released tables report cell size and tilt, so the rhombic-cap angle has to be measured from the volumes rather than read off a column.
Much of the X-ray material was built on experimental foundations, which may alter the base relative to natural comb.
assessments.rationale: The claim is a specific geometric description of one structure, the hive-bee cell, and open X-ray volumes of that structure exist. Prism geometry is already implicit in the hexagonal segmentations, and the diagnostic cap angle is measurable if the cell base was scanned. The foundation-comb caveat lowers adequacy without removing the possibility of a direct test.

assessments.operationalization: Combine comb geometry with construction sequences: test whether walls flow to the rhombic and hexagonal configuration while wax or pulp is semi-fluid and the insects only extrude close-packed tubes. Automatic attainment of the angles in bee-free semi-fluid wax would support the claim; active sculpting of the angles, or geometry that appears only where bees work the wall, would count against it.

candidate_datasets.name: Honeycomb X-ray microscopy
candidate_datasets.role: Three-dimensional records of how Apis mellifera changes cell geometry when the starting foundation size is altered, evidence about construction behaviour

obstacles: Finished angles are compatible with surface tension, with thermoplastic flow, and with behavioural building, so outcome geometry does not identify the agency.
Wasp paper comb and direct wax-temperature or surface-tension measurements are not in this honeybee deposit.
assessments.rationale: Public three-dimensional comb data show bees merging, tilting and layering cells as foundation size changes, which speaks to an active building process. They do not record wax fluidity or surface tension during wall formation, so the proposed automatic mechanism is only indirectly constrained. The rival of deliberate wax economy is likewise only partly addressed.

assessments.operationalization: Count faces and face shapes of interior cells in symmetrical, near-equal parenchyma. A mode near twelve rhombic faces would support the dodecahedral claim; a mode near fourteen with hexagonal and square faces would support Kelvin's tetrakaidecahedron instead.

candidate_datasets.name: Arabidopsis shoot-meristem segmentations
candidate_datasets.role: 3D cell segmentations from which face number and neighbour counts of interior cells can be computed

candidate_datasets.name: Arabidopsis embryo image collection
candidate_datasets.role: Embryo volumes whose interior cells can be segmented for the same face census

obstacles: Meristem and embryo cells are a young, growing subset of the symmetrical parenchyma the claim is about.
Surface cells must be excluded, because the twelve-versus-fourteen contrast is about interior cells of a bulk foam.
assessments.rationale: Face number is a clean discriminator between the rhombic dodecahedron and Kelvin's fourteen-sided cell, and public segmentations make the count feasible. Those segmentations are meristems and early embryos rather than mature equal-celled parenchyma such as pith. The ideal can be tested in a restricted tissue class and not yet across the stated scope.

assessments.operationalization: Ask whether late-cleavage geometry continues to satisfy the same minimal-surface and contact rules that fix the two- and four-cell stages, with no extra lineage-specific parameters. Late embryos whose contacts and angles match a surface-mechanics extrapolation would support that reading; stereotyped positions that violate those constraints would limit it.

candidate_datasets.name: SSBD
candidate_datasets.role: Quantitative image series of later cleavage in several animals

obstacles: Simple physical laws can be stretched to cover almost any material configuration, so the decision rule needs a pre-specified constraint set.
Fitting a full mechanical model of advanced cleavage is specialist work and is longer than a routine remeasurement.
assessments.rationale: Late-cleavage images are public and can be checked against the Plateau-type constraints developed for early stages, which is a fair partial reading of the claim. The assertion that the whole configuration is accurately determined by simple physical laws does not name which laws, and many outcomes fit both those laws and lineage-specific developmental programs. Only the restricted geometric continuation is testable now.

assessments.operationalization: At the four-cell stage, predict polar-furrow arrangement from relative blastomere volumes and compare that prediction with a model that assigns arrangements by clade. Arrangements tracking size ratios, with little phylogenetic signal once size is controlled, would support the claim; clade-conserved furrows at the same size ratios would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: SSBD
candidate_datasets.role: Quantitative early-embryo sets in which cell volumes and contact topology can be measured together

obstacles: Molluscs, annelids and coelenterates, where many of the classical furrow variants were drawn, are poorly represented in these databases.
Related species often share egg proportions, so size and classification are not fully independent.
assessments.rationale: Relative cell size versus furrow topology is a well-posed comparison, and it can be started on frog and sea-urchin volumes. The claim's scope is a cross-phylum distribution, and most of that comparative sample is still in uncompiled embryological plates. Phylogenetic non-independence of egg size is a real but manageable confound for the subset that is digitized.

assessments.operationalization: The claim asserts that no stage of development shows physical forces giving way to agencies outside physics. Any unexplained embryonic pattern is compatible both with physics not yet identified and with a vital agency, so no public measurement distinguishes the two.
obstacles: An agency unknown to physics has no separate observable that a dataset could record.
Failure to find a non-physical residue is not a confirming result under this wording.
assessments.rationale: This is a conceptual denial that vital agencies replace physical ones, not a statement with a measurable residue. Developmental image archives contain forms and genes and forces, and none of those variables marks the boundary the claim denies. Every empirical outcome can be read as still physical, so the claim cannot be confirmed or refuted by existing data.

assessments.operationalization: Among cells that are roughly rectangular and divide into near-equal daughters, test whether the new wall cuts the longest axis and whether the next wall is perpendicular to the previous one. That pattern would support the claim; equal divisions parallel to the long axis, or successive walls that are not orthogonal, would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: Arabidopsis embryo image collection
candidate_datasets.role: 3D wall-stained embryos for division-plane orientation against mother-cell axes

candidate_datasets.name: Arabidopsis shoot-meristem segmentations
candidate_datasets.role: Segmented meristem cells with successive division orientations

obstacles: Many cells in these volumes are not rectangular, so the test has to be restricted to the shape the rule assumes.
Tissue stress orients some divisions and can mimic or mask a pure longest-axis rule.
assessments.rationale: The longest-axis rule and the right-angle alternation are explicit and apply to a recognizable subset of cells in public embryo and meristem volumes. Standard geometric measurements can confirm or refute them for that subset within weeks. Adequacy is limited to model plants rather than rectangular dividing cells in general, which is still enough for the rule as a biological regularity.

assessments.operationalization: For symmetric divisions, compare the area of the observed partition with the least area that can divide the mother-cell volume, and with plausible larger alternatives such as a fixed genetic plane. Observed walls clustering on the area minimum would support Errera's rule; a systematic preference for a larger surface would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: Arabidopsis embryo image collection
candidate_datasets.role: Embryo volumes already used to compare observed division surfaces with geometric rules, including area minimization

candidate_datasets.name: Arabidopsis shoot-meristem segmentations
candidate_datasets.role: Meristem segmentations for the same area comparison in a growing tissue

obstacles: Several geometric rules nearly coincide in symmetric cells, so the test needs asymmetric and irregular mothers where the minimum is unique.
Computing a minimal surface is specialist but is an established method in this literature.
assessments.rationale: Errera's least-area rule is a direct comparison between an observed wall and a computable surface, and open embryo and meristem segmentations contain both the volumes and the walls. That comparison has already been framed on data of this kind and can be repeated or extended with current tools. Overlap with other geometric rules is a known bias and is reducible by choosing cells where the candidate surfaces differ.

assessments.operationalization: For unequal divisions of roughly cubical cells, plot partition shape against the volume fraction cut off. Curved corner walls below about three-tenths, and spherical octants below about 0.15, with plane walls above the threshold, would support the claim; plane walls remaining common below three-tenths would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: Arabidopsis embryo image collection
candidate_datasets.role: Embryo volumes that include unequal divisions whose volume fraction and wall curvature can be measured as a partial analogue

obstacles: Fucus hairs, moss paraphyses and stomatal precursors, the cases named for this corner geometry, are not in the embryo collection.
Two-dimensional sections underestimate the difference between a quarter-cylinder and a plane.
assessments.rationale: The volume thresholds are numerically explicit, so the pattern would be decisive if cubical cells with known daughter volumes were archived. Public embryo volumes offer some unequal divisions and not the corner-cutting geometry of the named hairs and precursors. The rule can be probed on a proxy tissue and cannot yet be resolved for the cells it was stated about.

assessments.operationalization: On quadrant-shaped flat cells, measure where the anticlinal wall meets the straight sides and what angle of arc it cuts off. An arc that meets both edges at right angles, cuts off about 55 degrees, and starts near three-tenths of the radius would support the claim; a straight radial wall or a periclinal wall in equal halves would refute it.
obstacles: Erythrotrichia discs and pressure-flattened frog or sea-urchin eggs are illustrated in classical plates, not in a public coordinate table.
The numerical arc and radius fractions need measured outlines rather than schematic drawings.
assessments.rationale: The predicted arc is specific enough that a modest set of quadrant cells would confirm or refute it. Those cells are not available as an open morphometric dataset, though published figures show the qualitative anticlinal curve. The quantitative constants are only partly checkable from existing images.

assessments.operationalization: Measure the apical angle of sector-shaped cells and whether the next wall is anticlinal or periclinal. Anticlinal walls concentrated between about 62.5 and 90 degrees, and periclinal walls in narrower sectors, would support the claim; anticlinal walls common in narrow sectors would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: Arabidopsis shoot-meristem segmentations
candidate_datasets.role: Segmented shoot apices in which wedge-shaped cells and the orientation of the next wall can be scored

candidate_datasets.name: Arabidopsis embryo image collection
candidate_datasets.role: Embryo cells with sector-like outlines for the same angle-versus-orientation test

obstacles: Meristem surface cells are polygonal prisms more often than the flat circular sectors the threshold was derived for.
Flattened discs and fern apices in the stated scope are mostly uncompiled.
assessments.rationale: The angular window is a sharp, refutable prediction, and some wedge-shaped cells in public apex and embryo volumes can be scored for wall orientation. Those cells are an imperfect match to the circular-sector geometry used to derive 62.5 degrees. The test is informative for growing points that have been segmented and incomplete for the wider scope.

assessments.operationalization: Follow a uniformly growing flat disc after a quadrant divides into a triangular and a quadrilateral daughter, and record which daughter divides next and at what radius. The triangular cell reaching division size first, near 1.35 times the starting radius against about 1.52 for the quadrilateral, would support the claim; simultaneous division, or the quadrilateral dividing first, would refute it.
obstacles: No public time-lapse of Erythrotrichia or a similar disc records daughter area against disc radius through the next division.
Fixed embryo collections cannot supply the division-time order this numerical prediction requires.
assessments.rationale: The claim predicts both an order of division and two radius ratios under uniform disc growth. That is a clean test and it needs live, cell-resolved growth of that geometry. Such a series is not in current open datasets, so the constants cannot be confirmed or refuted without new observations.

assessments.operationalization: In discoid embryos, algal discs and antheridia, test whether repeated divisions leave a peripheral layer of quadrilateral cells with radial walls, and whether a minimal-area division sequence reproduces that layer. A peripheral quadrilateral epidermis generated by that sequence would support the claim; a peripheral layer whose divisions do not follow the minimal-area order would weaken the proposed origin.

candidate_datasets.name: Arabidopsis embryo image collection
candidate_datasets.role: Early embryo volumes in which a peripheral cell layer and its division orientations can be inspected

candidate_datasets.name: BioImage Archive
candidate_datasets.role: Additional public images of embryonic and thalloid surfaces with an outer cell layer

obstacles: A quadrilateral epidermis can be produced by an identity program as well as by successive least-area divisions.
Moss embryos, algal discs and antheridia are sparsely represented next to Arabidopsis.
assessments.rationale: The finished pattern, a superficial file of parallel-sided cells, is visible in some open embryo volumes. Showing that the pattern is the residue of minimal-area divisions needs the division sequence or a model comparison tied to those cells. Existing data can check the pattern in a few systems and only partly test the proposed mechanism.

assessments.operationalization: Classify the surface partition pattern of many eight-cell frog eggs and test whether more than one topological type occurs at appreciable frequency. Several recurring arrangements within the species would support the claim; a single arrangement in nearly every egg would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: SSBD
candidate_datasets.role: Quantitative embryo datasets that include individually resolved cleavage stages

obstacles: Atlas images preferentially show a textbook arrangement, which is the sampling bias the claim is warning against.
A frequency count needs many individual eggs, and public atlases are not already tabulated that way.
assessments.rationale: Within-species variability of the eight-cell pattern is a direct frequency question, and frog cleavage images are public. They are not a random sample of eggs with arrangements already scored, so a small team would still be compiling rather than downloading a finished census. The test is well posed and only partly executable on what is archived.

assessments.operationalization: Classify surface eight-cell groups, animal and plant, into the thirteen topological types implied by three-way meetings and no submerged cell, and count exceptions. Every group that meets those premises falling into one of the thirteen types would support the empirical rider; a recurring surface arrangement that meets the premises and fits none of the types would refute the enumeration.

candidate_datasets.name: Arabidopsis embryo image collection
candidate_datasets.role: Plant embryos at stages with a small number of surface cells

obstacles: If the three-way and all-cells-on-the-surface premises hold, the thirteen types are a combinatorial list, and images cannot reveal a fourteenth type without breaking a premise.
Many real eight-cell groups include an internal cell or a transient four-way junction and so sit outside the claim's antecedent.
assessments.rationale: The enumeration is largely a theorem about partitions, and datasets test only whether real surface groups obey its premises and look like the listed types. Public cleavage and embryo images support that conformity check for a few organisms. They do not convert the combinatorial statement into an independent empirical law, which limits both discriminating power and scope.

assessments.operationalization: Rank eight-cell and similar small aggregates by how evenly contacts are distributed among the cells, and compare that rank with how often each arrangement occurs. Frequency falling as contact variance rises would support the claim; common arrangements in which one cell takes most of the contacts would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: SSBD
candidate_datasets.role: Individual embryo volumes suitable for contact graphs of small cell groups

candidate_datasets.name: Arabidopsis embryo image collection
candidate_datasets.role: Plant embryos for the same evenness-versus-frequency comparison

obstacles: Published figures over-sample arrangements authors considered normal, which can fake a stability ranking.
Oil-drop models mentioned alongside cells are not part of these biological archives.
assessments.rationale: Evenness of contacts and the frequency of each arrangement are both countable from cleavage volumes, and their correlation is a real prediction. The volumes are not a balanced sample across the types, and frequencies have not been deposited. A biased atlas can support a partial test and cannot yet establish which arrangements are the commonest in nature.

assessments.operationalization: Assemble partition topologies of small cell groups and of small organs across plants and animals, and test whether the same few graphs recur with weak phylogenetic signal. The same configurations in distant lineages, and relatedness adding little once topology is constrained, would support the claim; configurations clustering by clade would count against it.

candidate_datasets.name: Arabidopsis embryo image collection
candidate_datasets.role: Plant embryo partitions as the botanical side of the same comparison

obstacles: If only a few topologies are possible, recurrence is expected and does not by itself explain why those topologies were used.
Organs, as opposed to early cell groups, are not coded as partition graphs in these databases.
assessments.rationale: A three-lineage sample of early embryos can show whether a few cell-partition types are shared. That is a fragment of a claim that also covers organs and the whole of plants and animals, most of which is uncompiled. Shared topology is only weakly discriminating once the number of legal partitions is already small.

assessments.operationalization: Compare fossula geometry in rugose corals with the septal graphs expected from three-way meetings, and test whether fossulae co-vary with other bilateral organ systems. Fossulae that match packing variants and occur without a broader bilateral suite would support the space-partition reading; fossulae aligned with a conserved bilateral plane and other bilateral traits would leave the higher-organization reading standing.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: 3D scans of coral skeletons, some of which resolve septal contacts

candidate_datasets.name: iDigBio
candidate_datasets.role: Museum photographs of Heterophyllia, Zaphrentis and other rugose corals

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: Occurrence and taxonomic data for placing fossulate corals in a phylogenetic and stratigraphic sample

obstacles: Showing that a fossula is a legal three-way packing does not rule out a biological bilateral function for the same chamber.
Septal junctions are often obscured in photographs of abraded fossils, and side-by-side organ-grade characters are not coded for these genera.
assessments.rationale: Specimen images and scans can test whether fossulae look like ordinary completions of a trivalent septal network. The claim's denial that this indicates a higher bilateral grade is an inference about how the structure should be read, and packing compatibility does not uniquely decide it. Occurrence data help with sampling and do not supply the morphological test by themselves.

assessments.operationalization: Measure epidermal cell aspect ratio and the spatial arrangement of stomata on the same leaves. Stomata in rows where cells are oblong, and irregularly placed where cells are polygonal, including within lineages that break the monocot-dicot pairing, would support the claim.

candidate_datasets.name: Arabidopsis stomatal coordinates
candidate_datasets.role: Pixel coordinates of every stomate on 66 Arabidopsis leaves, for testing whether stomata on a polygonal epidermis are scattered rather than rowed

obstacles: The open coordinate table is Arabidopsis, a polygonal case, and does not include the oblong-celled monocot leaves that should show rows.
Monocots tend to have both oblong cells and stomatal files, so phylogeny and cell shape have to be separated.
assessments.rationale: Row versus scattered arrangement against cell shape is a clear spatial test, and one half of it, scattered stomata on a polygonal epidermis, can be measured from a deposited coordinate table. The oblong-cell, rowed half is widely illustrated and not similarly compiled. Phylogenetic confounding between grasses and files keeps even a future two-sided test from being automatic.

assessments.operationalization: Compare mature pollen and spore shape with whether the wall rigidified before the tetrad separated. Grains that hardened in the tetrad keeping plane facets and sharp angles, and grains that separated while soft becoming spherical, would support the claim; spherical grains that hardened in permanent tetrads, or angular grains that separated soft, would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: PalDat
candidate_datasets.role: Public pollen micrographs and shape descriptors, including pollen-unit type, for scoring spherical versus faceted grains and tetrad retention

obstacles: PalDat records shape and whether grains are united, not the developmental timing of wall hardening relative to separation.
Apertures, harmomegathy and drying also produce facets, and fern and red-algal spores are outside this pollen database.
assessments.rationale: Pollen shape and tetrad versus monad status are openly coded for a large angiosperm sample, which proxies the claim by asking whether retained tetrads are the faceted grains. The actual timing of solidification is in scattered ultrastructural studies, not in PalDat. Shape has several other causes, so the association is informative and confounded.

assessments.operationalization: At cryptogam apices, compare the frequency of buds and other outgrowths on triangular cells with the frequency on quadrangular cells, holding position on the apex constant. A higher outgrowth rate on triangular cells would support the claim; no bias, or a bias toward quadrangular cells, would refute it.
obstacles: Triangular cells often sit at the tip, so shape and the position where buds arise are collinear unless position is controlled.
Moss, liverwort, fern and algal apices are not gathered in one shape-by-outgrowth table.
assessments.rationale: A preference for outgrowths on triangular cells is a countable bias, and some apical images exist to start the count. Coverage of cryptogams is thin, and the classical anatomical plates are not a clean sample. Position is a serious confound because the cells the claim singles out also occupy the usual bud site.

assessments.operationalization: Record cell shape immediately before division and the plane that is used: transverse in markedly oblong cells, oblique when the cell is a little more than a hemisphere, and longitudinal when it is less than a hemisphere. That mapping, in cells whose shape was set by the growth-to-division interval, would support the claim; planes uncorrelated with those shape classes would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: Arabidopsis embryo image collection
candidate_datasets.role: Mother-cell shapes and daughter walls for a proxy test of the shape-to-plane map

candidate_datasets.name: Arabidopsis shoot-meristem segmentations
candidate_datasets.role: Meristem cells with geometry just before and after division

obstacles: Shape is partly defined by the growth-to-division ratio, so that half of the wording is close to a description of the cell that is about to divide.
The three-way rule was stated for moss, liverwort, fern and algal apical cells, which these Arabidopsis volumes only approximate.
assessments.rationale: The shape-to-plane mapping is measurable and overlaps rules that public embryo and meristem volumes were built to study. Those volumes are the wrong taxa for the apical cells named in the claim, so they test a proxy. The growth-rate clause adds little beyond the shape already observed, which caps how decisive a confirmation can be.

assessments.operationalization: From time-lapse of growing organs, compare the growth-rate anisotropy field with the orientation and timing of division planes, and with organ shape after divisions are reoriented or suppressed. The claim is supported if shape and division geometry are predicted by the growth field, and weakened if division orientation changes form while growth anisotropy stays fixed.

candidate_datasets.name: BioImage Archive
candidate_datasets.role: Open cellular imaging, including developmental time series from which growth and division can be measured in model organs.

obstacles: Growth and division are mechanically coupled, so a correlation does not by itself settle which is cause.
Open imaging covers a few model organs, not growing multicellular structures in general.
assessments.rationale: Direction of causation can be turned into a comparison of strain and division, but only after choosing what counts as a decisive perturbation. Suitable movies exist for Arabidopsis, Drosophila and a few other systems, scattered across imaging archives rather than as one growth-versus-division table. That sample can test the relation in those organs and cannot cover the stated scope of plants and animals, and analysis means harmonizing datasets before any causal contrast is credible.

assessments.operationalization: Score published ultrastructure of spicules, cartilage, bone, concretions and plant cell walls for whether the first mineral lies in extracellular matrix or cell wall rather than in active cytoplasm. A high extracellular fraction supports the rule; a large class of intracellular precipitation refutes it as a rule.

candidate_datasets.name: Cell Image Library
candidate_datasets.role: Reviewed cell micrographs, including extracellular matrix and mineral skeletons, for locating crystals relative to cytoplasm.

candidate_datasets.name: EMPIAR
candidate_datasets.role: Open electron and X-ray tomography that can show whether mineral is inside cells or in surrounding formed material.

obstacles: Dead or inactive tissue is not a label in image archives and has to be inferred from cell integrity.
Intracellular calcification, as in coccolithophores, is well known but unevenly archived relative to vertebrate bone.
assessments.rationale: The site of precipitation is a standard ultrastructural observation, so the rule is directly scorable where images resolve mineral and cytoplasm. Those images are spread through papers and image archives, with bone and a few protist groups far better covered than spicules and plant walls. A compiled subset can support or damage the rule, but assembling a taxonomically fair sample is months of work rather than a download-and-test.

assessments.operationalization: In published lime-free versus normal seawater rearings of echinoid embryos, score skeletal-rod presence, larval-arm length and survival. Suppression of rods and arms with continued development supports the claim; normal skeletons, or death rather than skeleton-less development, refutes it.
obstacles: The rearings are reported as figures in papers, not as a reusable open table of larvae, treatments and phenotypes.
Apparently healthy is loosely defined, and the published experiments cover a few echinoid species rather than skeleton-forming organisms generally.
assessments.rationale: Rods, arms and survival are an obvious confirming and refuting pattern, and the contrast with seawater controls is discriminating. The observations exist in the experimental literature, including later repeats of calcium-free culture, but they are not gathered in a public dataset that can be reanalysed as data. A literature compilation can test the claim for the species that were reared and cannot underwrite the broader extension.

assessments.operationalization: Test two proxies: whether sunlight reflected from the sea is sufficiently circularly polarized, and whether that polarization produces a measurable enantiomeric excess in relevant molecules. Either failure weakens the proposed starting force; success still leaves rival origins of biological homochirality standing.
obstacles: The wording is that asymmetry may have started this way, so a successful laboratory effect does not identify the historical cause.
Parity violation, chance amplification and other chiral biases predict the same biological handedness.
assessments.rationale: Only the physical adequacy of a non-living polarizing force is measurable with existing photochemistry and atmospheric optics, and those results sit in papers rather than in one open dataset. Nothing public records the polarization and chemistry of the prebiotic sea surface at the origin of homochirality. The hypothesis is therefore only weakly separable from other asymmetric forces, and only the proxy, not the origin, can be examined now.

assessments.operationalization: Compare sectioned pearls, molluscan and teleost otoliths, and albumin-precipitated calcospherites for concentric zoning and radial fabric. A shared geometry supports a common precipitation mode; systematic differences in zoning or crystal habit refute the identification.

candidate_datasets.name: AFORO
candidate_datasets.role: Open catalogue of teleost sagitta images and outlines, a partial view of otolith form rather than sectioned internal fabric.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: Downloadable micro-CT of biomineral specimens, usable where otolith or concretion volumes resolve internal zonation.

obstacles: Pearls and artificial calcospherites are mostly illustrated in papers, not in the otolith catalogues.
Similar concentric-radiate structure can arise from more than one precipitation chemistry.
assessments.rationale: The structural comparison is measurable, but the inference from shared structure to a shared physico-chemical mode is one interpretation among others. Otolith outlines are well archived, while matched sections of pearls, otoliths and laboratory calcospherites are not. A subset comparison is feasible from images and scans; it would not cleanly exclude other ways of building the same fabric.

assessments.operationalization: For scales, otoliths, bones and starch grains with known-age or known-environment series, test whether zone counts match day, season or other external periods. Zones that form without a matching external cycle support the claim that periodicity need not be external; a universal match would refute that caution.

candidate_datasets.name: PANGAEA
candidate_datasets.role: Published sclerochronology and otolith series that pair increment measurements with age or environmental time series.

obstacles: An endogenous oscillator can still lock to an external cycle, so agreement does not prove external cause.
Starch grains and most bones are poorly represented next to commercial fish otoliths and bivalve or coral bands.
assessments.rationale: The empirical content is that rhythmic zones are not necessarily calendars, and known-age hard parts can supply mismatches or matches. Increment series are public but scattered across PANGAEA deposits and papers, and they cover a subset of the structures named. Because the claim is a prohibition on assuming an external cause, one well-documented endogenous case is informative, while entrainment keeps many individual series ambiguous.

assessments.operationalization: Compare calcium carbonate and phosphate solubility in intact albumin versus its breakdown products, and test whether mineralization fronts in calcified tissues coincide with proteolysis rather than with carbonic-acid reaction on a more soluble salt. Precipitation tied to protein breakdown, and not to the acid route, would support the claim.
obstacles: No public dataset pairs local proteolysis, protein concentration and mineral appearance in calcifying tissues.
Modern mineralization also depends on phosphate supply and inhibitors, which the two historical mechanisms do not capture.
assessments.rationale: The chemical alternative is clear enough to test in vitro and at a mineralization front, but the needed paired measurements are not in an open resource. Older solubility remarks are scattered in the chemical literature and do not cover skeletal tissues at the stated scope. Discriminating the protein-breakdown route from carbonic-acid precipitation, among other controls now known to matter, would require new compiled measurements.

assessments.operationalization: Place skeletal elements on a size axis and test whether forms near cell size match surface-tension geometries while large bones match load trajectories, using curvature, junction angles and stress-alignment metrics. A change of regime with size supports the claim; the same controlling geometry at both scales refutes it.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: 3D scans spanning vertebrate bones and some small skeletal elements, for comparing form against size.

candidate_datasets.name: DigiMorph
candidate_datasets.role: Public CT slices of vertebrate skeletons whose size and load-bearing architecture can be measured.

obstacles: Surface tension versus muscle and gravity has to be inferred from form, and several mappings are possible.
Phylogeny and material change with size, and cell-sized spicules are scarce in CT archives built for bones.
assessments.rationale: Scale is measurable and the two regimes suggest different geometries, but the forces themselves are an interpretation of those geometries. Open scans cover large bones well and minute skeletons poorly, so only a biased slice of the size range can be compared. Even a clean size trend would leave material and ancestry as alternative explanations of the form difference.

assessments.operationalization: Reconstruct the spicule axis and test whether geodesic curvature on a spherical or ellipsoidal cell surface is indistinguishable from zero, predicting circular, elliptic or helical arcs. Systematic departure from a surface geodesic, or a fit only after implausible cell shapes are assumed, would refute the confinement rule.

candidate_datasets.name: World Porifera Database
candidate_datasets.role: Public taxonomic catalogue with linked sources for curved sponge spicules whose axes can be digitized from images.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoBank
candidate_datasets.role: Open morphology projects and images that include spicule form for some sponge matrices.

obstacles: The cell surface that confined growth is almost never preserved with the finished spicule.
Many published figures are drawings, and 2D projections underdetermine a space curve.
assessments.rationale: A geodesic on a stated surface is a sharp geometric prediction, and C- and S-shaped spicules can be digitized from existing images. What is missing is the cell at the time of growth, so the test becomes a fit to an assumed ellipsoid rather than a measured confinement. That proxy can reject gross mismatches and cannot separate a true geodesic from other curves that also look like circular or spiral arcs.

assessments.operationalization: Embed siliceous sponge spicules and calcareous holothurian spicules in a common morphospace and test whether corresponding forms overlap. Overlap supports form set by shared external confinement; separation that tracks mineralogy rather than shape class would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: World Porifera Database
candidate_datasets.role: Catalogue and linked images of siliceous sponge spicule types used as one side of the comparison.

candidate_datasets.name: World Register of Marine Species
candidate_datasets.role: Taxonomic entry point for holothurians as well as sponges, with links toward species whose spicules are illustrated in the literature.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoBank
candidate_datasets.role: Morphological matrices and media for coding spicule shape independently of skeletal chemistry.

obstacles: The two groups are not a controlled contrast: cell geometry and ancestry differ along with chemistry.
Quantitative spicule outlines are not in one downloadable table and would have to be measured from plates.
assessments.rationale: Form overlap versus mineral class is a fair empirical reading of the argument, and both spicule faunas are extensively illustrated. The illustrations are not a joint morphometric dataset, and holothurian and sponge images sit in different literatures. Similar shapes would still be compatible with convergence for reasons other than cell confinement, so the chemistry-independence claim is only partly separated from its rivals.

assessments.operationalization: Measure angles between rays of triradiate and four-rayed spicules. Equal cells should give 120 degree triacts and tetrahedral angles near 109 degrees; a distribution centered on 90 degrees or on no preferred angle would refute the junction rule, and unequal cells should widen that scatter.

candidate_datasets.name: World Porifera Database
candidate_datasets.role: Species-level access to calcareous and tetractinellid sponges whose triact and tetract spicules are illustrated.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoBank
candidate_datasets.role: Open images and character matrices from which inter-ray angles can be measured for sponge spicules.

obstacles: Most available views are 2D micrographs or drawings, which bias 3D tetrahedral angles.
There is no pre-measured angle table, so the sample has to be compiled from plates.
assessments.rationale: The angles are explicit and distinguish the junction hypothesis from orthogonal or random rays. Large numbers of triacts and tetracts have been figured, but they are not an open measurement dataset, and planar triacts are much easier to score than four-rayed spicules in space. A small team could test the 120 degree case from published images; the tetrahedral and unequal-cell clauses need 3D that is only partly available.

assessments.operationalization: Measure hexactinellid ray angles for cubic orthogonality versus the angles of closest packing, and, where tissue is preserved, score whether the vesicles around forming spicules are in linear cubic series. Orthogonal rays without cubic vesicle packing would leave the packing mechanism unshown.

candidate_datasets.name: World Porifera Database
candidate_datasets.role: Taxonomic access to hexactinellids and linked spicule illustrations for measuring ray orthogonality.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: 3D scans of sponge skeletal elements, sparse for glass sponges but usable where hexactine spicules are deposited.

obstacles: Soft-tissue vesicle packing at the moment of spicule formation is rarely preserved or archived.
Orthogonal silica rays can also be produced by crystal habit, not only by cubic cell packing.
assessments.rationale: Ray geometry is scorable from spicule images, but the claim is about the packing of the vesicles that moulded them. Public data are mostly cleaned spicules, not developmental histology, and they cover a modest fraction of hexactinellids in measurable 3D. Orthogonality is compatible with more than one mechanism, so a geometric pass would support only the form half of the claim.

assessments.operationalization: From occurrence tables, measure geographic range sizes, sample-level richness and evenness, and the stratigraphic span of families and genera, including whether living taxa are already present in the Cambrian. Cosmopolitan ranges, high local richness without single-species dominance, and Cambrian-to-Recent identity would support the claim; endemic ranges, dominance, or much later first appearances would refute the corresponding clause.

candidate_datasets.name: Neptune Sandbox Berlin archive
candidate_datasets.role: Downloadable deep-sea microfossil occurrences, including radiolarians, for co-occurrence, ranges and stratigraphic duration.

candidate_datasets.name: Ocean Biodiversity Information System
candidate_datasets.role: Living marine occurrence records for testing whether radiolarian species lack geographic limits.

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: Fossil occurrences through the Phanerozoic for testing Cambrian identity and long taxonomic ranges.

obstacles: Sampling effort and taxonomic lumping can mimic cosmopolitanism and high local richness.
Deep-sea drilling archives are strongest in the Cenozoic, so Paleozoic coverage depends on other occurrence compilations.
assessments.rationale: Range, dominance and first appearance are standard occurrence statistics, and radiolarians are present in open marine and fossil databases that a small team can query directly. Coverage is uneven between living plankton, deep-sea cores and Paleozoic rocks, but it is enough to confirm or refute worldwide ranges, local diversity and the Cambrian claim. Effort bias is real and is handled by rarefaction rather than by collecting new samples.

assessments.operationalization: Compare the grains in agglutinated tests with the surrounding sediment for size, shape and mineralogy, and ask whether the bias matches specific surface energies. A bias predicted by surface energy supports the physical account; a selectivity that surface energy does not predict is at least compatible with active choice.

candidate_datasets.name: PANGAEA
candidate_datasets.role: Sediment grain-size and foraminiferal assemblage tables that can be paired, where co-located, with test composition.

candidate_datasets.name: World Foraminifera Database
candidate_datasets.role: Taxonomic catalogue of agglutinated foraminifera, identifying the species whose grain selection has been described.

obstacles: Grain preference is predicted both by surface energy and by biological selection, so the same bias fits both.
Matched test-plus-sediment measurements are scattered in papers rather than linked in one archive.
assessments.rationale: Foreign particles in the test are observable, but volition versus surface energy is not a unique pattern in grain counts. Sediment and foraminiferal census data are public, while the particle-by-particle composition of tests is not systematically attached to them. Existing studies can test a subset of rhizopods and leave the mechanism underdetermined.

assessments.operationalization: On spherical lattice shells, measure the fraction of hexagonal meshes, node angles near 120 degrees, and whether irregularity of the mesh tracks irregularity that a vesicular foam would produce. Strong hexagonal order is consistent with groove collection; a different predominant polygon, or order unrelated to any foam, counts against that route.

candidate_datasets.name: Mikrotax
candidate_datasets.role: Image-based taxonomy of Cenozoic radiolarians, including lattice shells whose mesh geometry can be digitized.

obstacles: Finished skeletons do not preserve the surface vesicles that supposedly moulded the grooves.
Hexagonal nets are also expected from other physical models, including bubble packing and reaction-diffusion.
assessments.rationale: Mesh statistics are a direct geometric test and radiolarian lattices are extensively imaged in an open taxonomic system. The developmental step, silica collecting in grooves between vesicles, is not in those images. Hexagonal order can therefore support the form prediction for a well-illustrated subset of species while leaving the groove mechanism interchangeable with other pattern-forming processes.

assessments.operationalization: Apply one regularity metric, such as mesh-angle variance or deviation from a spherical hex net, to silica radiolarian lattices, strontium-sulphate acantharian skeletons and organic Clathrulina lattices. Equal regularity supports material-independence; regularity that tracks chemistry refutes it.

candidate_datasets.name: Mikrotax
candidate_datasets.role: Open images of radiolarian lattices, the silica side of the comparison, with much thinner coverage of acantharians and heliozoans.

obstacles: Acantharia dissolve and Clathrulina is not a focus of the radiolarian image archives, so the three materials are unequally documented.
Chemistry is confounded with clade, so equal regularity need not mean a shared vesicular mould.
assessments.rationale: A common regularity metric across the three named materials is a straightforward test of the independence claim. Silica lattices are well imaged; strontium-sulphate and organic lattices are mostly in separate papers and drawings. The available sample can compare a limited set of species, and phylogenetic confounding keeps a positive result from isolating the mould as the cause.

assessments.operationalization: On Callimitra and similar nassellarian skeletons, count interfaces and measure meeting angles against Plateau's laws: faces in threes near 120 degrees and edges near the tetrahedral angle. Agreement supports a four-cell interfacial origin; angles far from those values, or a different topology, refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: Mikrotax
candidate_datasets.role: Radiolarian images and taxonomic plates from which Callimitra-type skeletons can be measured.

obstacles: Many classical figures are schematic, and Haeckel-style drawings can impose the regularity being tested.
Angle agreement does not show that four living cells were present when the skeleton formed.
assessments.rationale: The soap-film angles and the tetrahedral graph are specific enough to accept or reject from specimens or faithful images, and the claim is limited to a small group of nassellarians. Public images exist but quantitative 3D of Callimitra is thin, so the testable object is mostly the drawn or photographed geometry. That can confirm the geometric match for this genus and cannot establish the cellular history the geometry is said to require.

assessments.operationalization: Measure face regularity of radiolarian pentagonal dodecahedra and icosahedra from specimens or scans. Confirmed regularity excludes an origin in crystallographic space-filling; irregular faces, or only those polyhedra that crystals allow, would remove the stated ground for rejecting a crystallization-like partition.

candidate_datasets.name: Mikrotax
candidate_datasets.role: Images of polyhedral radiolarian skeletons, including circoporid-type forms when figured, for testing face regularity.

obstacles: Thompson's premise relies on Haeckel's figures, which may have been regularized.
These skeletons are uncommon, so a regularity measurement will rest on few specimens.
assessments.rationale: Once regularity is measured, the crystallographic restriction does the rest of the work, so the empirical task is whether the dodecahedra and icosahedra are actually regular. Images exist, but they are few, often drawings, and not a 3D morphometric series of Circoporidae. A modern subset can test the geometric premise and cannot by itself rule out every non-crystalline space-partitioning process.

assessments.operationalization: Measure the latitudes and counts of the twenty spines. Hexagonal symmetry predicts two polar spines, six equatorial spines and two alternating whorls of six; Müller's arrangement predicts five four-spine circles and no polar spine. A systematic match to one angular template and not the other decides the claim.

candidate_datasets.name: Mikrotax
candidate_datasets.role: Radiolarian skeleton images from which spine positions can be digitized where twenty-spined forms are figured.

obstacles: Acantharia, the main living twenty-spined group, are poorly represented in polycystine image databases and their skeletons are rarely preserved.
Older sources are drawings that may already embody one or the other symmetry scheme.
assessments.rationale: The two arrangements make different, quantitative predictions, so spine coordinates would discriminate them cleanly. What is public is a scatter of figures rather than a downloadable angle table, and the best-preserved illustrations are not a random sample of living Acantharia. The test is standard once images are compiled, but current open archives only partly cover the named genera.

assessments.operationalization: No outcome cleanly separates an unexplained central polarity, said to be perhaps like fluid-crystal directive forces, from other ways of placing a fixed set of spines. Locating the first sign of polarity in the central cytoplasm would address only that geographical clause.
obstacles: Absence of an obvious mechanical force is not a measurement with a refuting result.
Central origin, cortical origin and several molecular polarities can leave the same adult spine map.
assessments.rationale: The passage states that no obvious mechanical account is available and points to fluid crystals as a direction in which to look, which does not fix variables or a decision rule. Adult skeletons show the polarity without showing where it was generated or which force class produced it. Existing images are compatible with the suggestion and with its rivals, so the claim as stated is not an empirical contrast.

assessments.operationalization: On cylindrical vessels, tracheids and insect tracheae, classify wall thickenings as annular, longitudinal or helical and test whether helices have constant pitch. All three geodesic families, with constant-pitch helices, support the identification; spirals whose pitch varies along the cell refute the helical geodesic.

candidate_datasets.name: BioImage Archive
candidate_datasets.role: Open microscopy of plant and animal tissues, including xylem and tubular cells whose wall thickenings can be traced.

candidate_datasets.name: Cell Image Library
candidate_datasets.role: Annotated cell images for scoring annular, longitudinal and spiral wall patterns on cylinders.

obstacles: On a cylinder, rings, generators and constant-pitch helices are the geodesics, so the label adds little once the pattern is named.
Quantitative pitch series are sparse compared with textbook illustrations of the three types.
assessments.rationale: Occurrence of the three thickening types is standard anatomy and can be checked in public micrographs of vessels and tracheae. Calling them geodesics is then almost a theorem, so the result does not separate the claim from ordinary anatomical description except where pitch is non-constant. Images suffice for a qualitative survey and not for a high-powered discrimination.

assessments.operationalization: Unroll or fit the suture and parallel striae of high-spired shells such as Turritella on a cone and test whether they are conical geodesics whose coils tighten toward the apex. A constant-pitch helix, or coils that do not close apically, would refute the stated curve.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: 3D scans of gastropod shells from which the sutural curve can be extracted and fit as a geodesic.

candidate_datasets.name: iDigBio
candidate_datasets.role: Specimen photographs of turreted gastropods for measuring how suture spacing changes toward the apex.

candidate_datasets.name: Digital Atlas of Ancient Life
candidate_datasets.role: Open fossil-shell illustrations, including high-spired gastropods, for the same sutural measurement.

obstacles: Photographs give a profile of the suture; a full geodesic test is more secure on 3D scans, which are fewer than photos.
Ornament and repaired breaks can locally displace the suture from the growth curve.
assessments.rationale: Tightening coils on a cone are a specific alternative to a constant-pitch helix or to the shell's own logarithmic spiral, and both photographs and scans of Turritella-like shells are public. Coverage is good for common high-spired genera and thinner for the full diversity of turreted forms. Fitting the curve is a standard morphometric job on the order of weeks.

assessments.operationalization: Sample reticulated patterns on cell walls and integuments and test what fraction are two opposite constant-pitch helices rather than cracks, vessels or reaction-diffusion nets. A high fraction of crossed geodesics supports the claim that they are a common source; a minority would refute commonness.

candidate_datasets.name: BioImage Archive
candidate_datasets.role: Micrographs of cell surfaces and integuments on which reticula can be classified.

candidate_datasets.name: iDigBio
candidate_datasets.role: Specimen images of organisms whose external reticulate patterns can be sampled, though usually at coarser resolution.

obstacles: Common source requires a defined universe of patterns, and several generators make similar criss-cross textures.
The scope is all curved organic surfaces, far beyond any one image collection.
assessments.rationale: Crossed helices can be recognized on individual images, but the claim is about how common that origin is among reticulated patterns. Public images touch pieces of that universe and do not inventory it. Even a careful sample would leave other pattern-forming processes as live alternatives wherever the geometry is only approximately helical.

assessments.operationalization: On reconstructed surfaces of heart, stomach, arteries and gut, compare muscle-fiber trajectories with computed geodesics. Fibers lying on shortest paths, annular and longitudinal on a simple tube, support the claim; systematic extra length or a non-geodesic helix would refute it for that organ.

candidate_datasets.name: Human cardiac diffusion MRI dataset
candidate_datasets.role: Open cardiac diffusion-tensor imaging and derived myocardial orientation maps for testing fiber paths against geodesics.

candidate_datasets.name: Cardiac Atlas Project
candidate_datasets.role: Ventricular shape models on which surface geodesics can be computed and compared with fiber directions.

obstacles: Open fiber-orientation data are concentrated on the human left ventricle, not the stomach, arteries, intestine or worm body wall.
Myocardial fibers also follow sheet architecture and load, so a geodesic fit can be confounded with stress alignment.
assessments.rationale: Shortest paths on a measured surface are a clear test, and public cardiac diffusion data plus ventricular shape models make the heart part feasible with specialist but existing tools. The claim names a list of hollow organs for which comparable open fiber maps are sparse. A heart-only result would resolve a restricted scope and leave the general automatic-arrangement claim open.

assessments.operationalization: Test whether adult heart and stomach fibers are geodesics of the twisted surface, whether oblique gastric fibers match a new pouch geodesic, and whether pump performance requires that shortest-path layout. Adult geodesic fits support only the geometric residue of the developmental claim.

candidate_datasets.name: Human cardiac diffusion MRI dataset
candidate_datasets.role: Adult human myocardial fiber orientations, a proxy for the post-twist heart but not a developmental series.

candidate_datasets.name: Cardiac Atlas Project
candidate_datasets.role: Adult ventricular geometry used to compute geodesics; it does not record the primitive tube or the stomach.

obstacles: Remaining geodetic after twisting requires the fiber map through development, which these adult datasets do not contain.
Effective contraction is compatible with non-geodesic architectures, so function does not isolate the shortest path as necessary.
assessments.rationale: The adult heart can be checked for geodesic fibers, which is only the end state of a developmental claim about dilatation, twisting and new gastric systems. Open data are adult ventricular diffusion and shape, not a series from the primitive tube and not a comparable stomach dataset. The further claim that the heart works only because fibers take the shortest course is not separated from other working architectures by these measurements.

assessments.operationalization: From 3D tracks, measure body rotation, path curvature and whether the trajectory is a helix about a nearly straight axis rather than a circle. A helix whose turning matches axial rotation supports the swerve-averaging account; circular paths without rotation, or helices produced without body rotation, refute it for that swimmer.

candidate_datasets.name: Dryad bilophotrichous bacterial tracks
candidate_datasets.role: Open 3D swimming trajectories that include helical paths, for a bacterial subset of small swimmers.

candidate_datasets.name: BioImage Archive
candidate_datasets.role: Cell-motility imaging that can supply tracks for additional flagellates and ciliates where deposited.

obstacles: The clearest open 3D tracks are bacteria, whereas the claim centers on ciliates, flagellates, rotifers and swarm-spores.
A helical flagellar beat can draw a helix without a constant body-fixed swerve.
assessments.rationale: Helix versus circle, tied to measured body rotation, is a direct and discriminating test, and some open 3D tracks already exist. They represent a slice of small swimmers rather than the full list of ciliated and flagellated organisms. Reanalysis of those tracks is standard; extending the same test to rotifers and typical ciliates depends on imaging that is only partly archived.

assessments.operationalization: Fit logarithmic spirals against Archimedean, Fermat and other curves on ruminant horns, mollusc and foraminiferan shells, and sunflower floret parastichies, and fit the cordate leaf outline as the stated exception. A logarithmic spiral uniquely among those forms, and a poor log-spiral fit to the cordate leaf, supports the claim.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: 3D shells and some horns whose outlines can be fit to spiral models.

candidate_datasets.name: iDigBio
candidate_datasets.role: Specimen images of shells, leaves and sunflower heads for outline and parastichy fits.

candidate_datasets.name: Mikrotax
candidate_datasets.role: Foraminiferal shell images for the same logarithmic-spiral test.

obstacles: Sunflower parastichies are often treated as Fermat spirals, so the curve family has to be fit rather than assumed.
Horn scans and digitized leaf outlines are less uniformly available than mollusc photographs.
assessments.rationale: Competing spiral equations are standard to fit, and public images or scans exist for every class the claim names, including the cordate-leaf exception. Taxonomic depth is greatest for molluscs and thinner for horns and capitula, but a decisive mismatch in any named class would refute the universal. The curve-fitting itself is ordinary morphometrics on existing pictures.

assessments.operationalization: The empirical residue is whether a force that turns with the growing body, identified with the columellar muscle in snails, is what produces the spiral, as opposed to an external field of constant direction. That requires force or muscle-activity measurements during growth, not shell outline alone.
obstacles: Shell shape is compatible with any intrinsic asymmetry of growth and does not identify the columellar muscle as the deflecting force.
No public dataset records muscle force through shell coiling.
assessments.rationale: That a fixed external direction cannot wind a growing structure into a spiral is a kinematic argument, not a dataset result. The biological claim that the co-rotating force is the columellar muscle needs measurements that have not been archived. Shell collections can show that spirals exist and cannot show which force produced them or exclude other intrinsic growth asymmetries.

assessments.operationalization: Along growth lines of tubular shells and horns, measure the ratio of longitudinal to transverse extension and the spiral angle. A ratio that stays constant and matches the angle supports the claim; a drifting ratio that still yields a logarithmic spiral, or a constant ratio that does not, refutes it.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: Shell and horn scans with growth increments from which the two rates and the spiral angle can be measured.

candidate_datasets.name: iDigBio
candidate_datasets.role: Photographs of coiled shells whose whorl expansion can be compared with the tangent angle.

obstacles: Horns are less often scanned with usable growth lines than mollusc shells.
Within an ideal logarithmic model the ratio and the angle are linked by definition, so the empirical test is constancy on real specimens.
assessments.rationale: Constancy of the growth-rate ratio, and its match to the spiral angle, can be read from increments on existing shells. Public scans and photographs cover common molluscs well enough to accept or reject the relation, with horns as a thinner additional scope. The measurement is standard geometric morphometrics and does not need new collections.

assessments.operationalization: On scorpioid cymes, measure successive shoot lengths and divergence angles and test whether the shoots are tangents to a logarithmic spiral. A constant length ratio and equal angles support it; varying ratios that miss the spiral refute it. The helicoid case additionally requires recovering a spiral after removing the twist.

candidate_datasets.name: iDigBio
candidate_datasets.role: Herbarium images of borages and other cymose plants from which shoot lengths and angles can be digitized.

obstacles: Pressed specimens flatten the helicoid twist, so the hidden spiral is not recoverable from a typical sheet.
Shoot lengths are not pre-measured; each inflorescence has to be digitized from a photograph.
assessments.rationale: The scorpioid prediction is a concrete length-and-angle pattern, and herbarium photographs of the relevant families are public in large numbers. They are 2D and flattened, so they can test the scorpioid tangent spiral and not the claim that a helicoid cyme hides the same curve. Digitizing a sample is feasible but is compilation rather than a ready-made analysis.

assessments.operationalization: Compare shape of successive whorls or growth stages of spiral shells, horns and other terminally accreted structures, scaling them to the same size. Persistent shape supports growth without change of form; systematic ontogenetic allometry refutes it.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: 3D shells and horns on which successive whorls can be scaled and compared.

candidate_datasets.name: iDigBio
candidate_datasets.role: Large photographic samples of coiled shells for an ontogenetic shape test.

obstacles: Aperture damage and sculpture can masquerade as shape change.
Some groups are photographed mostly as adults, so early whorls are less often measurable.
assessments.rationale: Isometry of successive increments is a standard outline comparison, and shells with visible whorls are abundant in open image and scan collections. The claim is general for spiral shells and similar terminal growth, and the public sample is broad enough that widespread allometry would refute it while widespread isometry would support it. The analysis is routine geometric morphometrics.

assessments.operationalization: For shells, opercula, foraminiferal chambers, horns and tusks, test whether each growth increment is a scaled copy of the whole pre-existing outline. Increments that leave the enlarged form similar support the gnomon claim; increments that change the shape refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: Scans of accreted hard parts with growth boundaries that can be tested for gnomonic similarity.

candidate_datasets.name: Digital Atlas of Ancient Life
candidate_datasets.role: Illustrated fossil shells and chambers for comparing each added increment with the previous whole.

obstacles: Gnomonic growth is mathematically close to the logarithmic spiral, so the test largely travels with the self-similarity test.
